objectives: Explain computational neuroscience as a cycle of questions, data, models, and inference, rather than equating it with programming or the application of machine-learning algorithms.
Distinguish descriptive, mechanistic, and normative models, and select an appropriate level of model for a given neuroscience question.
Starting from a minimal input–output model, write testable predictions, residuals, and a parameter-estimation objective, and explain how each quantity is obtained experimentally.
Organize the mathematical, programming, and neuroscience prerequisites into an actionable learning loop: know when to calculate, when to plot, and when to return to the biological hypothesis.
prerequisiteBridge: Here, “computation” means more than a computer executing instructions. It also includes the transformations by which the brain turns sensory inputs into estimates, decisions, and actions. Begin by treating a system as a black box with inputs and outputs: a visual stimulus enters, and neuronal spikes or a behavioral choice emerge. The course will open that box gradually, proposing internal variables and interactions and testing those hypotheses against data. If you can read graph axes and understand how a function maps one number to another, you already have the mathematical starting point for the first lecture.

A model is a purposeful simplification of a question, not a miniature copy of reality. A map omits individual trees yet remains useful for navigation; likewise, a threshold-linear model omits ion channels yet can test whether stronger stimulation raises firing rate. Judge a model first by the question it serves, then by whether omitted factors could change the answer. That judgment matters more than memorizing model names and prevents complexity from being mistaken for realism.

Parameters, probability, and optimization recur throughout the course. Parameters are unknown numbers in a model, such as stimulus gain w and baseline b. Probability expresses uncertainty across repeated trials. Optimization searches candidate parameters for the set that best explains the data. High-school algebra, function graphs, and averages are enough to begin; derivatives and matrices can be added when they arise. Use the same learning loop each time: state the hypothesis in words, write the symbols, calculate one numerical example, plot the prediction, and inspect the residuals. If a plot conflicts with expectation, check axes, units, parameters, and data splitting before changing the scientific hypothesis.

diagnostic.prompt: Researchers record firing rate r at several sound intensities s. Identify the input and output, and propose a minimal testable hypothesis.
diagnostic.answer: The input is sound intensity s and the output is firing rate r. One testable hypothesis is \(r=\max(0,ws+b)\), where w is the intensity gain and b is the baseline offset.
diagnostic.explanation: Naming the variables is not enough: a testable hypothesis must specify their relationship and allow data to contradict it. If firing rate saturates as intensity rises, for example, the threshold-linear relationship will leave systematic residuals.

diagnostic.prompt: “A more complex model is closer to the truth, so it must be better.” What is wrong with this claim?
diagnostic.answer: Model quality depends on the question, the amount of data, and testability. Extra degrees of freedom may merely memorize noise without improving predictions on new data.
diagnostic.explanation: A complex model can fit more shapes, but it can also be harder to interpret, estimate, and falsify. Compare out-of-sample prediction, parameter uncertainty, and whether the omitted mechanisms matter for the current question.

diagnostic.prompt: If ten repetitions of the same stimulus produce ten different responses, does that directly refute a deterministic input–output model?
diagnostic.answer: No. A deterministic model may describe the conditional mean response, while observation noise or a probabilistic model describes trial-to-trial variation.
diagnostic.explanation: First specify whether the model predicts a single-trial response or an average response. Only after separating the mean trend from the fluctuations can you decide whether a discrepancy belongs to the mean model or the noise model.

diagnostic.prompt: If a model underestimates firing rate for every large stimulus, what pattern should the residuals show, and what should you do next?
diagnostic.answer: Residuals remain positive at large stimulus values, so the errors are not scattered randomly. Examine the gain, nonlinear shape, or missing variables instead of reporting only an overall mean squared error.
diagnostic.explanation: A systematic dependence of residuals on input is diagnostic. A residual-versus-stimulus plot usually localizes model failure more clearly than a single score.

modules.title: From interdisciplinary backgrounds to answerable questions
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does computational neuroscience require neuroscience, physics, mathematics, and engineering together rather than any one discipline alone?
paragraphs: The instructor's background across neurobiology, physics, and applied mathematics reveals the field's working pattern. Experiments define the nervous-system objects and constraints. Mathematics compresses verbal hypotheses into relationships that can be derived. Computation extends those derivations beyond hand-calculable scales. Engineering forces models to produce operational outputs. These are not four unrelated labels; they form a chain from observation to explanation to test.

Consider the question “How does an animal judge motion direction?” Neuroscience selects the area to record and the stimulus and behavioral measures. Mathematics defines stimulus direction s, neural response n, and choice y. A model proposes \(P(n|s)\) or \(P(y|n)\). A program estimates parameters and compares predictions. Code without a well-defined question cannot generate a scientific explanation automatically; biological description without quantitative relationships cannot distinguish competing mechanisms.

Interdisciplinary work often breaks at the level of terminology. “Encoding,” for example, might mean that mean firing rate changes with a stimulus, or that a full conditional distribution carries information. Repair the ambiguity by replacing nouns with observables and operations: hold stimulus s fixed, repeat the trial to obtain responses n, ask whether the distribution of n changes with s, and measure how accurately s can be estimated after observing n. Once the claim is operationalized, the disagreement has a calculable target.

Three levels of explanation recur in this field. A descriptive model summarizes a pattern in data, such as a tuning curve. A mechanistic model proposes components that generate the pattern, such as ion channels or network connections. A normative model asks for the best strategy for a task, such as maximum-likelihood decoding. The three levels may give different answers for the same phenomenon; choose among them according to the question, not the length of the equation.
keyPoints: Interdisciplinary value comes from a testable chain of work, not a list of disciplinary labels.
Rewrite a scientific question in terms of inputs, outputs, repeatable conditions, and comparable predictions.
Descriptive, mechanistic, and normative models answer questions at different explanatory levels.

derivation.title: Turn a verbal question into a testable chain
derivation.setup: Let s denote a motion stimulus, n a neural response, and y a behavioral choice. The goal is to separate how the stimulus affects neural activity from how neural activity affects behavior.

steps.title: Define the observations
steps.explanation: For each trial with fixed stimulus s, record neural response n and behavior y. Repeat the trial to obtain conditional samples instead of retaining a single observation.

steps.title: Factor the relationship
steps.explanation: The general chain rule is \(P(n,y|s)=P(y|n,s,\phi )P(n|s,\theta )\). The first factor simplifies to \(P(y|n,\phi )\) only under the additional assumption that the recorded n fully mediates the effect of s on y—that is, y and s are conditionally independent given n. This Markov assumption must be tested; it is not a probability identity.
steps.latex: P(n,y\mid s)=P(y\mid n,s,\phi)P(n\mid s,\theta)\xrightarrow{\;y\perp s\mid n\;}P(y\mid n,\phi)P(n\mid s,\theta)

steps.title: Generate a prediction
steps.explanation: Estimate \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) from one portion of the data, then calculate response or choice probabilities for new trials that were not used in estimation and compare them with observed frequencies.

steps.title: Locate the failed stage
steps.explanation: If the neural-response prediction succeeds but the behavioral prediction fails, the readout relationship is the likely problem. If the response prediction itself fails, revise the encoding hypothesis or the stimulus variables.

symbolNotes: s is the experimentally controlled stimulus, n is a neural response that may be a count or vector, and y is the behavioral outcome.
\(\theta\) and \(\phi\) parameterize the two model stages; a hat marks a value estimated from training data.
\(y\perp s|n\) states conditional independence: once n is known, s provides no additional information for predicting y. The assumption often fails when the neural recording is incomplete.
derivation.unitsCheck: Probability is dimensionless and lies between 0 and 1. A count n is dimensionless, but its counting window must be stated explicitly in seconds or milliseconds.
derivation.limitCheck: If n is completely unrelated to s, \(P(n|s)\) is identical for every s, so the response cannot discriminate stimuli. If \(P(y|n,s)\) still changes substantially with s after conditioning on n, the simplified \(s\to n\to y\) Markov chain fails and must include a missing neural state or direct stimulus pathway.

workedExample.title: Split a perception problem into two tests
workedExample.problem: Present 50 motion trials in each direction. A neuron produces an average of 12 spikes for rightward motion and 5 for leftward motion. A threshold \(n\ge 9\) predicts “right”; 38 rightward trials and 7 leftward trials cross threshold. Calculate accuracy and identify which part of the model this rule tests.
steps: The rule correctly classifies 38 rightward trials; the remaining 12 are incorrectly labeled left.
For leftward motion, \(50-7=43\) trials remain below threshold, so 43 trials are classified correctly.
The total is \(38+43=81\) correct trials out of 100, for an accuracy of 81%.
The difference in means supports an effect of stimulus on response. The 81% accuracy tests whether a specific readout rule can convert the response into a stimulus judgment.
workedExample.result: This threshold decoder has accuracy 0.81. That does not prove that the brain uses the same threshold, but it supplies a comparable decoding baseline.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Accuracy must lie between 0 and 1. Swapping every left/right label would give 19%, and the two accuracies sum to 100%.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is “this brain region activates during the task” not yet a mechanistic explanation?
selfCheck.answer: It reports only that activity and task co-occur. It does not specify the variables, connections, or dynamics that generate the activity, nor does it predict quantitatively how an intervention should change it.

pitfalls: Treating “uses a computer” as a sufficient definition of computational neuroscience while ignoring models and scientific questions.
Inferring a causal mechanism from correlated activity without proposing predictions that an intervention or new data could test.

modules.title: Four core questions and the model–data loop
modules.guidingQuestion: How can broad questions about sensory extraction, body control, memory, and intelligence be reduced to one computable and falsifiable study?
paragraphs: The second page groups the field's targets into extracting information from sensation, controlling the body, forming memories, and producing intelligent behavior. Each is too broad until an object, time scale, and observable are specified. “How does vision work?” can become “How does the spike count of an MT neuron change with coherence during a 200 millisecond random-dot-motion stimulus?” Narrowing the question does not diminish it; it links theory to experiment.

The model–data loop has five repeatable actions: define variables, write relationships, estimate parameters, predict held-out data, and inspect the error structure. In \(r(s)=\max(0,ws+b)\), s is stimulus intensity, r is mean firing rate, w controls slope, and b is the extrapolated intercept at zero stimulus. Data must constrain the parameters, and predictions must target observations that were not used for fitting.

Error is evidence for what to do next, not a nuisance outside the model. For stimulus \(s_{i}\), define residual \(e_{i}=r_{i}-\hat{r}_{i}\). Residuals scattered without pattern around zero reveal no obvious systematic bias in the mean relation. Persistently positive residuals at large stimuli suggest missing upward curvature or another input. Residual magnitude that grows with the mean suggests that the noise model must change. Different shapes motivate different revisions.

Simulation, data analysis, machine learning, and mathematical modeling play distinct roles in the loop. Simulation generates consequences of a specified model. Data analysis summarizes and displays observations. Machine learning can uncover high-dimensional predictive relationships. Mathematical modeling emphasizes the logical path from assumptions to results. A study may use all four, but each step needs explicit inputs, outputs, and evaluation criteria so that a high prediction score does not conceal a wrong interpretation.
keyPoints: Reduce a broad question to an executable one by specifying the object, time window, manipulated variable, and observable.
After parameter estimation, evaluate predictions on data that were not used for fitting.
Residual structure tells you whether to revise the mean relationship, the noise model, or the set of variables.

derivation.title: Minimal prediction and diagnosis with a threshold-linear model
derivation.setup: Given stimulus s and observed mean firing rate r, use \(\hat{r}=\max(0,ws+b)\) to represent a neuron that is silent below threshold and increases linearly above threshold.

steps.title: Find the threshold
steps.explanation: When \(w>0\), the linear term crosses zero at \(ws+b=0\), so the stimulus threshold is \(s_{0}=-b/w\).

steps.title: Write the piecewise prediction
steps.explanation: For \(s\le s_{0}\), the model predicts \(\hat{r}=0\); for \(s>s_{0}\), it predicts \(\hat{r}=ws+b\). The piecewise form makes the threshold interpretation explicit.

steps.title: Calculate residuals
steps.explanation: For every data point, compute \(e_{i}=r_{i}-\hat{r}_{i}\). A positive residual means that the model underpredicts; a negative residual means that it overpredicts.

steps.title: Compare candidate models
steps.explanation: If adding saturation lowers training error, also compare error on held-out stimuli or trials. Otherwise, the new parameter may only absorb training noise.

symbolNotes: w has units of firing rate divided by stimulus units; b and r are both measured in Hz.
\(\max(0,z)\) returns 0 when z is negative and z when z is positive; it does not mean the maximum response in the dataset.
derivation.unitsCheck: ws and b must both have units of Hz before they can be added. The residual \(r-\hat{r}\) is also measured in Hz.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(w=0\), response does not vary with stimulus. If \(b\ge 0\) and \(w>0\), the nonnegative stimulus range may contain no visible threshold.

workedExample.title: Calculate threshold, predictions, and residuals by hand
workedExample.problem: Let \(w=4 \mathrm{Hz}/unit\) and \(b=-8 \mathrm{Hz}\). At stimuli \(s=1\), 3, and 5, the observed mean firing rates are 1, 5, and 15 Hz. Calculate the threshold, predictions, and residuals.
steps: The threshold is \(s_{0}=-b/w=8/4=2\), so \(s=1\) is below threshold while \(s=3\) and 5 are above it.
The predictions are \(\max(0,4-8)=0\), \(\max(0,12-8)=4\), and \(\max(0,20-8)=12 \mathrm{Hz}\).
The residuals \(r-\hat{r}\) are \(1-0=1\), \(5-4=1\), and \(15-12=3 \mathrm{Hz}\).
Residuals increase with stimulus, suggesting that the true gain may exceed 4 or that the relationship bends upward at high stimulus values.
workedExample.result: The threshold is 2; predictions are 0, 4, and 12 Hz; residuals are 1, 1, and 3 Hz.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Every prediction is nonnegative, the linear segment begins at zero at threshold, and units remain Hz throughout.

selfCheck.prompt: A model fits its training set well but predicts new stimuli poorly. What does that tell you most directly?
selfCheck.answer: The model or estimation procedure has not captured a generalizable relationship. It may have too many degrees of freedom, inadequate training coverage, or omitted variables that change under the new stimuli.

pitfalls: Reporting only a correlation coefficient or training error without plotting predictions and residuals against stimulus.
Interpreting machine-learning prediction accuracy automatically as discovery of a neural mechanism.

modules.title: From model language to neural dynamics
modules.guidingQuestion: How can mathematics and programming serve understanding instead of becoming two additional subjects detached from neuroscience?
paragraphs: The sequence is deliberate: establish model language, study single-neuron dynamics, then move to neural coding, populations, and networks. Every stage reuses earlier tools. Vectors become population responses, differential equations become membrane voltages and synaptic currents, and probability becomes spike counts and decoding. The foundational ideas remain active throughout the course.

MATLAB or Python can serve as the programming language; syntax preference is secondary to performing the same scientific actions: create variables with units, calculate from equations, plot a check, vary parameters, and save a reproducible experiment. For a first implementation, verify the code with a hand-calculable example. Predictions for three points should match pencil-and-paper results before you expand the grid or the number of trials. Small examples guard against mistakes in symbols, indices, and units.

Flipped learning requires exposure before class, but “I watched it” is not a completion criterion. A stronger standard is to perform four tasks without prompts: answer the guiding question in your own words, reconstruct one derivation, solve one numerical example, and identify at least one condition under which the model fails. If one step breaks, return to the corresponding section and repair it rather than replaying everything from the beginning.

Keep a model record with the scientific question, variables and units, equations, parameter meanings, initial conditions, outputs, testable predictions, and known limitations. When a new model appears, compare it directly with the previous one. Perfect integrate-and-fire and leaky integrate-and-fire differ by one leak term, yet that term creates a steady state and rheobase current. Also record an experimental manipulation that could distinguish the two. Repeated comparison builds transferable understanding better than isolated memorization.
keyPoints: Foundational tools recur at the levels of single neurons, coding, and networks.
Verify code against a small hand-worked example before increasing scale or changing parameters.
Completion means being able to reconstruct, calculate, interpret, and state the model's boundaries.

workedExample.title: Design a twenty-minute model-learning loop
workedExample.problem: You need to study \(r=\max(0,3s-6)\) with only paper, pencil, and any programming environment. Give a short verifiable workflow and calculate the response for \(s=0\), 1, 2, and 4.
steps: State in words: below threshold the response is zero; above threshold each additional stimulus unit raises the response by 3 Hz.
By hand, the linear term 3s−6 equals −6, −3, 0, and 6. After nonnegative rectification, the responses are 0, 0, 0, and 6 Hz.
Enter only these four inputs in the program and print the outputs, confirming exact agreement with all four hand calculations.
Then plot the curve from \(s=0\) to 5, mark threshold \(s=2\), and note two boundaries: the model has no saturation and no trial-to-trial variability.
workedExample.result: The verified prediction is \([0,0,0,6]\) Hz, accompanied by a verbal explanation, hand calculation, code check, plot, and limitation check.
workedExample.sanityCheck: At \(s=2\) the linear term is exactly zero. For every increase of 1 in s above threshold, response should rise by 3 Hz.

selfCheck.prompt: Why begin with a hand-calculable example before running a large simulation?
selfCheck.answer: It provides an independent expectation and quickly exposes errors in indices, signs, units, and boundary conditions. A smooth-looking large plot does not prove that an implementation matches its equations.

pitfalls: Treating executable code as correct without checking it against independent values or limiting cases.
Rereading in page order without attempting to reconstruct derivations, examples, and failure conditions.

objectives: Determine the shape of each scalar, vector, or matrix before carrying out addition, inner products, outer products, matrix multiplication, or element-wise multiplication, and explain what the result represents.
Use a determinant to decide whether a given two-by-two matrix is invertible, calculate its inverse by hand, and verify that the product is the identity matrix.
From a probability mass function or density, calculate normalization, means, variances, marginals, and conditional distributions, and distinguish “uncorrelated” from “independent.”
Derive Bayes' rule from the two factorizations of a joint probability and distinguish the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior clearly.
prerequisiteBridge: A vector can be understood first as an ordered column of numbers—for example, one neuron's responses under two conditions. A matrix is a table of numbers whose row and column meanings are preserved. Before calculating, write the shape beside every object: a column vector \(u\in \mathbb{R}^{2}\) is \(2\times 1\), while \(A\in \mathbb{R}^{4\times 2}\) is \(4\times 2\). The inner dimensions must match in matrix multiplication because each row of the left matrix forms an inner product with each column of the right object. The outer dimensions determine the answer's shape. This rule prevents more errors than memorizing isolated calculations.

Probability describes patterns of outcomes across repeated trials. A discrete variable uses sums of probabilities; a Bernoulli variable, for example, takes only 0 or 1. A continuous variable uses integrals of a density. Density at a point may exceed 1, but probability—the area over an interval—must lie between 0 and 1. The mean is the long-run average location, and variance is the mean squared distance from that location. Conditional probability restricts the sample space after information is known; it is not synonymous with causation.

MATLAB notation is not identical to mathematical notation: `*` performs matrix multiplication, `.*` multiplies corresponding elements, and an apostrophe transposes a real matrix. Software may permit implicit expansion between a scalar and matrix, but abstract matrix addition still requires matching shapes. Use three checks for every computation: write the shapes, predict a sign or order of magnitude, then verify an independent identity—for example, \(B\cdot B^{-1}\) should be close to the identity. Use the same discipline in probability: check normalization and range, then recompute by marginalization or a complementary event.

diagnostic.prompt: A has shape \(4\times 2\) and v has shape \(2\times 1\). Are both Av and vA defined? If so, what is the shape?
diagnostic.answer: Av is defined and has shape \(4\times 1\). vA is undefined because the 1 column of v does not match the 4 rows of A.
diagnostic.explanation: Check the inner dimensions first. In Av, 2 matches 2 and the outer dimensions \(4\times 1\) remain. Reversing the order changes both compatibility and meaning.

diagnostic.prompt: Why is \(C=[[3,4],[6,8]]\) not invertible? Give a reason that does not depend on a software error.
diagnostic.answer: The second row is 2 times the first, so the rows are linearly dependent. Equivalently, \(\det(C)=3\cdot 8-4\cdot 6=0\), and no inverse exists.
diagnostic.explanation: Dependent rows mean that distinct inputs collapse to the same output. Once that information is lost, the output cannot recover a unique input. A zero determinant is the algebraic statement of the same fact.

diagnostic.prompt: An exponential distribution has rate \(\lambda =5 \mathrm{s}^{-1}\). What is the probability that the waiting time exceeds 0.2 s?
diagnostic.answer: \(P(X>0.2)=\exp(-\lambda \cdot 0.2)=\exp(-1)\approx 0.368\).
diagnostic.explanation: The exponential survival function is \(\exp(-\lambda x)\). The product of \(\lambda\) and time is dimensionless, as an exponential argument must be.

diagnostic.prompt: When does “zero covariance implies independence” hold, and why is it false in general?
diagnostic.answer: It holds for jointly Gaussian variables. For a general distribution, zero covariance rules out only linear co-variation; nonlinear dependence may remain.
diagnostic.explanation: For example, let X be symmetric about zero and let \(Y=X^{2}\). Then \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[X^{3}]-E[X]E[X^{2}]=0\) even though knowing X determines Y exactly.

modules.title: Start with shape: scalars, vectors, matrices, and products
modules.guidingQuestion: Why should a matrix calculation begin by writing every object's shape and the meaning of its rows and columns, rather than by substituting numbers?
paragraphs: Start with concrete objects: \(s=2\), \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), \(w=(0,1,2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), and matrices A, B, and C. These are more than arithmetic exercises: a vector may represent responses from several neurons, and a matrix may represent a linear map from stimulus to response. Shape records the input and output slots. If you ignore it, you may swap neuron and condition indices even when the arithmetic itself is correct.

Vector addition requires equal lengths and proceeds component by component. The inner product \(u^{\mathrm{T}}v\) maps two equal-length vectors to a scalar and can measure overlap in a common coordinate system. The norm \(||w||_{2}\) is the square root of \(w^{\mathrm{T}}w\) and gives Euclidean distance from the origin. The outer product \(uv^{\mathrm{T}}\) maps two vectors to a matrix whose i,j entry is \(u_{i}\) \(v_{j}\), retaining every pairwise combination. Do not confuse it with the inner product.

Interpret Av as the inner product of each row of A with v. If A is \(4\times 2\) and v is \(2\times 1\), the result is \(4\times 1\), with each output component a weighted sum of two input components. Matrix product BC pairs every row of B with every column of C. Matrix multiplication is generally noncommutative: even when BC and CB have the same shape, they may have different values and represent transformations in different orders.

Keep the abstract rule separate from language behavior. In MATLAB, `B*C` is matrix multiplication and `B.*C` is element-wise multiplication; for a real vector, `v'` produces a row vector. Some versions permit s+A by implicitly adding the scalar to each entry. That is an array-language convention, not ordinary addition between linear-algebra objects of different shapes. State explicitly which meaning your code uses.
keyPoints: Matrix multiplication requires matching inner dimensions and retains the outer dimensions.
An inner product is a scalar; an outer product is a matrix. They retain different information.
Software implicit expansion must be distinguished conceptually from abstract matrix addition.

derivation.title: Calculate a specified matrix product from its entrywise definition
derivation.setup: Let \(A=[[0,0.5],[10,1],[2,9],[2,7]]\) and \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\). Calculate Av while tracking its shape.

steps.title: Check compatibility
steps.explanation: A is \(4\times 2\) and v is \(2\times 1\). The inner dimensions 2 match, so the product exists and has shape \(4\times 1\).

steps.title: Calculate the first two rows
steps.explanation: The first row gives \(0\cdot 2+0.5\cdot 5=2.5\), and the second gives \(10\cdot 2+1\cdot 5=25\).

steps.title: Calculate the last two rows
steps.explanation: The third row gives \(2\cdot 2+9\cdot 5=49\), and the fourth gives \(2\cdot 2+7\cdot 5=39\).

steps.title: Assemble and verify
steps.explanation: In row order, the result is the column vector \((2.5,25,49,39)^{\mathrm{T}}\). Its four outputs correspond one-to-one with the four rows of A.

symbolNotes: The columns of A correspond to two input features, and its rows correspond to four output channels.
The transpose symbol \(^{\mathrm{T}}\) converts a column vector into a row vector without changing component order.
derivation.unitsCheck: If A is dimensionless and every component of v has the same unit, Av has the same unit as v. If the two columns represent different physical quantities, their weights must carry the appropriate conversion units.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(v=0\), then Av must be the zero vector. If one row of A is entirely zero, the corresponding output must be zero.

workedExample.title: Distinguish the inner product, outer product, and norm
workedExample.problem: Given \(u=(0,1)^{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(v=(2,5)^{\mathrm{T}}\), calculate u+v, \(u^{\mathrm{T}}v\), \(uv^{\mathrm{T}}\), and \(||v||_{2}\).
steps: Component-wise addition gives \(u+v=(2,6)^{\mathrm{T}}\).
The inner product is \(0\cdot 2+1\cdot 5=5\), a scalar.
The outer product is \([[0\cdot 2,0\cdot 5],[1\cdot 2,1\cdot 5]]=[[0,0],[2,5]]\), with shape \(2\times 2\).
The norm is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(2^{2}+5^{2})=\operatorname{sqrt}(29)\approx 5.385\).
workedExample.result: The sum is \((2,6)^{\mathrm{T}}\), the inner product is 5, the outer product is \([[0,0],[2,5]]\), and the norm is approximately 5.385.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The norm must exceed the largest component magnitude 5 and be smaller than the sum of component magnitudes 7; 5.385 satisfies both bounds.

selfCheck.prompt: Why can each output of A v be read as a weighted sum of one row of weights and the input?
selfCheck.answer: By definition, matrix multiplication gives \(y_{i}=\sum _j A_{ij} v_{j}\). Once output row i is fixed, the sum runs only over input index j, so that row lists how the output weights each input.

pitfalls: Multiplying whenever two objects have the same number of entries, without checking the inner dimensions required by matrix multiplication.
Confusing `*` with `.*`, which can produce the expected shape but a different scientific meaning.

modules.title: Identity, transpose, inverse, and singularity
modules.guidingQuestion: When can a matrix recover the input uniquely from the output, and why does a zero determinant prevent that recovery?
paragraphs: The identity matrix I has 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere and plays the role of scalar 1: \(Ix=x\). Transpose \(A^{\mathrm{T}}\) swaps rows and columns. Thus, if A maps a two-dimensional input to a four-dimensional output, \(A^{\mathrm{T}}\) has shape \(2\times 4\), but it is generally not the inverse of A. An inverse \(A^{-1}\) must satisfy \(A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I\) and exists only for a square, one-to-one mapping.

For a two-by-two matrix \(B=[[a,b],[c,d]]\), \(\det(B)=ad-bc\). Geometrically, the determinant is the signed area scale factor of the linear map. A zero determinant means that a two-dimensional region is compressed into a line or point, so distinct inputs yield the same output. Once the map flattens information, output alone cannot identify the original input and no inverse exists. This is the same fact as linear dependence among rows or columns.

For \(B=[[4,4],[8,9]]\), \(\det(B)=36-32=4\), so \(B^{-1}=(1/4)[[9,-4],[-8,4]]\). Verification matters more than calling `inv`: multiplying by B should give 1 on the diagonal and 0 off the diagonal. In numerical work, a nonzero determinant that is very close to zero may still produce an inverse that amplifies tiny errors dramatically. Check the condition number instead of stopping at “the software returned an answer.”

The Hadamard product B⊙C multiplies corresponding entries and requires equal shapes; the matrix product BC sums along a shared index. The first may represent channel-wise gain, while the second composes transformations. Calling both simply “multiplication” erases model structure. In a code audit, describe the objects on both sides of every multiplication sign and verify the first entry by hand.
keyPoints: An inverse recovers the input uniquely from the output; a transpose does not serve that purpose.
A zero determinant means that a map compresses dimensions and loses recoverable information.
A Hadamard product is element-wise, whereas a matrix product sums over the shared dimension.

derivation.title: The two-by-two inverse formula and numerical verification
derivation.setup: Find the inverse of \(B=[[4,4],[8,9]]\) and verify it by multiplying in both orders.

steps.title: Calculate the determinant
steps.explanation: \(\det(B)=4\cdot 9-4\cdot 8=4\). Because it is nonzero, the inverse exists.

steps.title: Swap and negate
steps.explanation: For a two-by-two inverse, swap the main-diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries, and divide by the determinant.

steps.title: Check the first row
steps.explanation: In \(B\cdot B^{-1}\), the first-row, first-column entry is \((4\cdot 9+4\cdot (-8))/4=1\). For the first-row, second-column entry, the two numerator terms are \(4\cdot (-4)\) and \(4\cdot 4\); after division by 4, the result is 0.

steps.title: Check the second row
steps.explanation: The second-row, first-column entry is \((8\cdot 9+9\cdot (-8))/4=0\), and the second-row, second-column entry is \((8\cdot (-4)+9\cdot 4)/4=1\), giving I.

symbolNotes: \(\det(B)\) is a scalar, and \(B^{-1}\) has the same shape as B.
The denominator \(\det(B)\) explains why the formula fails when the determinant is zero.
derivation.unitsCheck: If B maps units X to units Y, its entries carry Y/X and \(B^{-1}\) carries X/Y; their dimensionless product is I.
derivation.limitCheck: As the second row approaches a constant multiple of the first, \(\det(B)\) approaches zero, inverse entries grow in magnitude, and small observational errors are amplified.

workedExample.title: Compare matrix and element-wise multiplication
steps: The first row of BC is \(4\cdot 3+4\cdot 6=36\) and \(4\cdot 4+4\cdot 8=48\).
The second row is \(8\cdot 3+9\cdot 6=78\) and \(8\cdot 4+9\cdot 8=104\).
The element-wise product is \([[4\cdot 3,4\cdot 4],[8\cdot 6,9\cdot 8]]=[[12,16],[48,72]]\).
Both results have shape \(2\times 2\), but the first composes linear transformations while the second weights corresponding positions.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Every entry of BC is a sum of two products; every Hadamard entry is one product of corresponding elements.

selfCheck.prompt: Which distinct inputs does \(C=[[3,4],[6,8]]\) map to the same output, and how does that demonstrate noninvertibility?
selfCheck.answer: Because \(C(4,-3)^{\mathrm{T}}=(0,0)^{\mathrm{T}}\), any x and \(x+a(4,-3)^{\mathrm{T}}\) have the same output. The output cannot determine a, so it cannot recover a unique input.

pitfalls: Treating a nonzero determinant as sufficient for numerical stability and ignoring error amplification near singularity.
Using `inv(B)*y` instead of a more stable linear solve and failing to verify the result.

modules.title: From Bernoulli and exponential distributions to joint Gaussians and Bayes
modules.guidingQuestion: How do we move from uncertainty in one variable to dependence between two variables, then use observations to infer a hidden cause?
paragraphs: A Bernoulli variable X takes only 1 or 0 with probabilities p and 1−p. Its mean is \(E[X]=p\) because \(1\cdot p+0\cdot (1-p)=p\). Since \(X^{2}=X\), its variance is \(E[X^{2}]-E[X]^{2}=p-p^{2}=p(1-p)\). This can represent whether a spike occurs in a time window or whether a choice is correct. Counts across multiple windows form a binomial distribution only if trials are independent and share the same p.

The exponential density \(f(x)=\lambda \exp(-\lambda x)\), \(x\ge 0\), describes waiting times in a constant-rate Poisson process. Integration gives \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\), so the survival probability is \(\exp(-\lambda x)\). The mean and standard deviation are both \(1/\lambda\), the median is \(\ln 2/\lambda\), and the mode is 0. A mean larger than the median reflects the long right tail. Treating \(\lambda\) as the mean waiting time gives both a dimensional and numerical error.

A bivariate Gaussian is determined completely by its mean vector and covariance matrix. Integrating out one variable gives a Gaussian marginal; fixing an observation and renormalizing gives a Gaussian conditional distribution. Conditioning shifts the mean and reduces variance to the uncertainty left after accounting for the correlation. The derivation below gives the conditional mean, conditional variance, and Bayesian reweighting, allowing you to calculate the complete distribution rather than merely infer the tilt of an ellipse.

Bayes' rule follows from two factorizations of one joint probability: \(P(A,B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A)\). Rearrangement gives \(P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)\). In parameter inference, A may be parameter \(\theta\) and B the data D. Then \(P(D|\theta )\) is the likelihood, \(P(\theta )\) the prior, \(P(D)\) the normalizing evidence, and \(P(\theta |D)\) the posterior. A likelihood is not a probability distribution over the parameter unless it is multiplied by a prior and normalized.
keyPoints: Bernoulli variance \(p(1-p)\) is zero at \(p=0\) or 1 and maximal at \(p=1/2\).
Exponential rate \(\lambda\) and mean waiting time \(1/\lambda\) are reciprocals.
For jointly Gaussian variables, zero covariance implies independence; general distributions do not share this guarantee.
Bayes' rule is a rearrangement of two factorizations of the joint probability.

derivation.title: From conditioning a bivariate Gaussian to Bayesian reweighting
derivation.setup: Let \((X_{1},X_{2})\) be jointly Gaussian with mean \((\mu _{1},\mu _{2})\), standard deviations \(\sigma _{1}\) and \(\sigma _{2}\), correlation c, and \(|c|<1\). First obtain the full distribution of \(X_{1}|X_{2}=x_{2}\), then connect this continuous conditioning problem to Bayes' rule.

steps.title: Write the mean and covariance
steps.explanation: Diagonal entries are variances, while each off-diagonal entry is the correlation coefficient times both standard deviations.

steps.title: Calculate the determinant and inverse
steps.explanation: The factor \(1-c^{2}\) in the determinant determines whether the covariance is degenerate. The negative off-diagonal entries of the bivariate inverse create the conditional-mean correction when the Gaussian exponent is completed to a square.

steps.title: Marginalize first
steps.explanation: Integrating over the full range of \(x_{1}\) removes that dimension. The marginal of a bivariate Gaussian remains a univariate Gaussian with \(\operatorname{mean} \mu _{2}\) and variance \(\sigma _{2}^{2}\).

steps.title: Take a slice at the observed value
steps.explanation: Fix \(X_{2}=x_{2}\) in the joint density and absorb every factor depending only on \(x_{2}\) into the normalizing constant. The remaining exponent in \(x_{1}\) is still quadratic.

steps.title: Complete the square to obtain the conditional mean
steps.explanation: Completing the square in \(x_{1}\) shifts the center along the correlation direction. With positive correlation and \(x_{2}\) below its own mean, the conditional mean also shifts downward.

steps.title: Read off the conditional variance
steps.explanation: The quadratic term after completing the square gives the remaining variance. Knowing \(X_{2}\) reduces uncertainty from \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) to \(\sigma _{1}^{2}(1-c^{2})\).

steps.title: Write the full conditional distribution
steps.explanation: A one-dimensional Gaussian requires both a mean and a variance; the conditional distribution is incomplete unless both are stated.

steps.title: Connect to Bayes' rule
steps.explanation: Both continuous densities and discrete probabilities update by conditioning through two factorizations of the same joint quantity. The denominator is the evidence obtained by summing or integrating over every candidate cause.

symbolNotes: c is the correlation coefficient. A nondegenerate bivariate Gaussian requires \(|c|<1\); when \(c=0\), the variables are independent.
\(\mu _{1}|_{2}\) is the conditional mean after observing a specific \(x_{2}\), and \(\sigma _{1}|_{2}^{2}\) is the conditional variance. Report both.
The Bayesian denominator \(P(B)\), or \(p(x_{2})\), renormalizes the result. The continuous case uses densities rather than point probabilities.
derivation.unitsCheck: c is dimensionless. Multiplying \(\sigma _{1}/\sigma _{2}\) by \((x_{2}-\mu _{2})\) yields units of \(X_{1}\). Conditional variance and \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) both have squared \(X_{1}\) units. Normalization preserves the appropriate units for probabilities and probability densities.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(c=0\), the conditional mean returns to \(\mu _{1}\) and the conditional variance to \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\). As \(|c|\to 1\), the nondegenerate model approaches a line, conditional variance approaches zero, and the covariance matrix becomes singular.

workedExample.title: Two normalizations: a conditional Gaussian and low-base-rate Bayes
workedExample.problem: A: \(\mu _{1}=0\), \(\mu _{2}=1\), \(\sigma _{1}=0.5\), \(\sigma _{2}=1\), \(c=0.7\), and \(x_{2}=0.75\). Find the conditional mean, variance, and standard deviation of \(X_{1}\). B: disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity is 0.9, and false-positive rate is 0.05. Find the probability of disease after a positive result.
steps: For A, the conditional mean is \(0+0.7\cdot 0.5\cdot (0.75-1)=-0.0875\).
The conditional variance is \(0.5^{2}(1-0.7^{2})=0.25\cdot 0.51=0.1275\), so the conditional standard deviation is approximately 0.3571.
Because correlation is positive and \(x_{2}\) is below \(\mu _{2}\), the conditional mean falls below \(\mu _{1}\). The conditional variance 0.1275 is also smaller than the marginal variance 0.25.
For B, the joint probability of a true positive is \(0.9\cdot 0.01=0.009\), and that of a false positive is \(0.05\cdot 0.99=0.0495\).
The total probability of a positive result is \(0.009+0.0495=0.0585\).
The posterior probability after a positive result is \(0.009/0.0585\approx 0.1538\), or about 15.4%.
workedExample.result: A: conditional mean −0.0875, variance 0.1275, and standard deviation about 0.357. B: probability of disease after a positive result about 15.4%.
workedExample.sanityCheck: In A, the mean moves in the direction implied by the observation and conditional uncertainty decreases. In B, the posterior exceeds the 1% prior but remains far below the 90% sensitivity.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is \(P(D|\theta )\), viewed as a function of \(\theta\), called a likelihood but not equal to \(P(\theta |D)\)?
selfCheck.answer: The likelihood fixes the observed data and compares how well parameter values explain them. The parameter posterior must also incorporate a prior and normalize across every candidate parameter; the two expressions condition in opposite directions.

pitfalls: Treating a continuous density \(f(x)\) as a point probability \(P(X=x)\), even though probability comes from integration over an interval.
Confusing \(P(A|B)\) with \(P(B|A)\), especially by ignoring the prior in a low-base-rate setting.
Generalizing zero correlation to independence for arbitrary distributions.

objectives: Translate the statement “the rate of change depends on the current state and input” into a first-order differential equation, and explain why an initial condition is part of a complete prediction.
Derive the exact constant-input solution of \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\) by hand and verify it using the initial value, long-time limit, and units.
Derive the Euler update from the definition of a derivative, state the step-size condition for stability, and distinguish discrete numerical error from continuous-system behavior.
Rewrite a second-order oscillator as two first-order equations, interpret its state-space trajectory, and audit the piecewise boundaries and indices in the supplied MATLAB code.
prerequisiteBridge: Begin by reading \(dx/dt\) as “change in state divided by change in time” over a very short interval. A differential equation asks for an entire function \(x(t)\), not a single number: its slope at every time must obey the stated rule. A slope rule usually permits many shifted or scaled trajectories, so the state at one time, such as \(x(0)=x_{0}\), must also be specified. This is like starting from different points on the same road map: the route rule is unchanged, but later positions differ. Arrows in a phase portrait give local directions, and the initial condition chooses where motion along the flow begins.

The key property of \(e^{at}\) is that differentiation returns the same function times a constant: \(d(e^{at})/dt=a e^{at}\). It decays when \(a<0\) and grows when \(a>0\). A time constant \(\tau\) must carry units of time so that \(t/\tau\) is dimensionless. After one \(\tau\), a decaying exponential retains \(e^{-1}\approx 0.368\) of its initial value; after about \(3\tau\), it retains about 5%. This numerical intuition lets you judge the approach to steady state without relying on a plot.

A numerical simulation replaces a continuous trajectory with states at discrete times. Euler's method assumes that the current slope remains fixed throughout one step \(\Delta t\), so the next value equals the current value plus “step size × current slope.” A smaller step is usually more accurate but requires more calculations. A step that is too large can create oscillation or divergence absent from the continuous system. When reading code, keep four descriptions aligned: the continuous equation, the discrete update, parameter units, and boundary conditions. Compare at least two step sizes at the same physical time.

diagnostic.prompt: Both \(x=e^t\) and \(x=2e^t\) solve \(dx/dt=x\). What information is still missing?
diagnostic.answer: An initial condition is missing. Once \(x(0)=x_{0}\) is given, the coefficient is fixed at \(x_{0}\) and the solution becomes unique.
diagnostic.explanation: The differential equation constrains local slopes; the initial condition selects one trajectory from the allowed family. An equation without an initial value usually cannot make a unique numerical prediction.

diagnostic.prompt: For \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\), what is the sign of the derivative when \(x>I\), and in which direction does the state move?
diagnostic.answer: Because \(-x+I<0\), \(dx/dt<0\): x decreases toward the steady state I.
diagnostic.explanation: A slope field gives the direction without solving the equation. The state rises when \(x<I\), falls when \(x>I\), and has zero slope at \(x=I\).

diagnostic.prompt: For the no-input Euler update \(x_{n+1}=(1-\Delta t/\tau )x_{n}\), when does the sequence decay instead of diverging?
diagnostic.answer: Require \(|1-\Delta t/\tau |<1\), or \(0<\Delta t/\tau <2\). If sign alternation must also be avoided, require \(0<\Delta t/\tau \le 1\).
diagnostic.explanation: Each discrete step multiplies the state by amplification factor a. Convergence of the magnitude requires \(|a|<1\), while \(a<0\) creates sign alternation that the continuously decaying system does not have.

diagnostic.prompt: A forward-Euler simulation of an undamped oscillator spirals outward. Does that prove that the physical amplitude grows?
diagnostic.answer: No. The continuous system conserves energy, whereas the forward-Euler update matrix has a modulus greater than 1 at every finite step. The outward spiral is introduced by the numerical method.
diagnostic.explanation: Compare a continuous invariant, results at different step sizes, and a numerical method better suited to oscillators. A simulation plot reflects both the equation and the algorithm; it is not the equation alone.

modules.title: From a rate of change to the exact solution of a first-order system
modules.guidingQuestion: How can a local slope rule determine a complete time trajectory, and how can we verify that the resulting function satisfies both the equation and the initial value?
paragraphs: The examples \(dx/dt=x\) and \(d^{2}x/dt^{2}=-x\) show that a differential equation specifies a dynamical rule. A candidate solution is checked by substitution, not by visual resemblance. The derivative of \(x=e^t\) is \(e^t\), satisfying the first equation; the second derivative of \(x=\sin t\) is \(-\sin t\), satisfying the second. Initial conditions then select the amplitude and phase.

In \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\), \(\tau\) is the response time constant and I is constant input. Write the right-hand side as −(x−I): the steady state is \(x^{*}=I\), with positive slope below I and negative slope above I. Let \(y=x-I\) be the deviation from steady state. The equation becomes \(\tau  dy/dt=-y\), converting a constantly driven problem into pure exponential decay.

Separate variables to obtain \(dy/y=-dt/\tau\). Integration gives \(\ln|y|=-t/\tau +C\), and exponentiation gives \(y=Ae^{-t/\tau }\). Since \(y(0)=x_{0}-I\), \(A=x_{0}-I\) and \(x(t)=I+(x_{0}-I)e^{-t/\tau }\). The expression combines the steady state I with a fading memory of the initial condition; understanding those two terms matters more than memorizing the formula.

Apply three independent checks to the exact solution. Initial value: at \(t=0\) the exponential is 1, giving \(x_{0}\). Equation: differentiation gives \(\tau  dx/dt=-(x_{0}-I)e^{-t/\tau }\), equal to −x+I. Long time: as \(t\to \infty\) the exponential vanishes and \(x\to I\). You can also verify the initial slope \((I-x_{0})/\tau\). Failure of any check rules out the candidate for this initial-value problem.
keyPoints: A differential equation determines a trajectory only when paired with an initial condition.
For constant input, the steady state is I and the deviation x−I decays exponentially.
The initial value, substitution into the equation, and the long-time limit provide three independent checks of the exact solution.

derivation.title: Step-by-step solution of a first-order linear system with constant input
derivation.setup: Solve \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\) for \(x(0)=x_{0}\), assuming \(\tau >0\) and constant I.

steps.title: Find the steady state and shift variables
steps.explanation: Setting the derivative to zero gives \(x^{*}=I\). Define \(y=x-I\); because I is constant, \(dy/dt=dx/dt\).

steps.title: Separate variables
steps.explanation: Substitution gives \(\tau  dy/dt=-y\). Wherever y is nonzero, rearrange to \(dy/y=-dt/\tau\); \(y=0\) itself is the steady-state solution.

steps.title: Integrate and exponentiate
steps.explanation: Integrating both sides gives \(\ln|y|=-t/\tau +C\). Absorb the sign into the constant to write \(y=A \exp(-t/\tau )\).

symbolNotes: \(x(t)\) is a time-varying state. In this derivation, I is simply a constant input and does not necessarily mean electrical current.
\(\tau >0\) determines the decay rate, and \(x_{0}\) is the state at \(t=0\).
derivation.unitsCheck: x, I, and \(x_{0}\) must have the same units. \(dx/dt\) has state/time units, multiplication by \(\tau\) restores state units, and \(t/\tau\) is dimensionless.
derivation.limitCheck: Smaller \(\tau\) produces more decay over the same t. If \(x_{0}=I\), the exponential coefficient is zero and the system remains at steady state from the start.

workedExample.title: Calculate a step response over several time constants
workedExample.problem: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x_{0}=0\), with input held at \(I=5\) after \(t=0\). Calculate x at \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\) and 30 ms, and find the first time x reaches 4.
steps: The exact solution is \(x(t)=5+(0-5)e^{-t/10}=5(1-e^{-t/10})\).
workedExample.result: \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\approx 3.16\), \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\approx 4.75\), and x reaches 4 after approximately 16.1 ms.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The trajectory must rise monotonically from 0 without exceeding 5. All three results satisfy that condition, and reaching 80% of steady state takes about \(1.61\tau\).

selfCheck.prompt: If the input switches suddenly from \(I=5\) to \(I=-2\), which part of the solution changes? Does x jump instantly to −2?
selfCheck.answer: The new steady state is −2, and the value of x at the switching time becomes the new initial condition. A continuous first-order state does not jump; it approaches −2 exponentially with time constant \(\tau\).

pitfalls: Dropping the integration constant and thereby losing the ability to satisfy an arbitrary initial condition.
Treating \(\tau\) as a finite deadline at which steady state is reached; an exponential approaches its limit only asymptotically.

modules.title: Euler's method: from the derivative definition to a stable step size
modules.guidingQuestion: How does a discrete update approximate continuous dynamics, and why can step size determine stability as well as accuracy?
paragraphs: The derivative definition gives \(dx/dt\approx [x(t+\Delta t)-x(t)]/\Delta t\). Substitute it into \(dx/dt=f(x,t)\) and evaluate the right-hand side at the current time to obtain forward Euler: \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\Delta t f(x_{n},t_{n})\). The method extends the current tangent by one step, so error arises because the true slope changes during that interval. Local error per step is usually of order \(\Delta t^{2}\); over a fixed total time, global error is of order \(\Delta t\).

For \(\tau  dx/dt=-x+I\), Euler gives \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}+(\Delta t/\tau )(-x_{n}+I)\). Define \(\alpha =\Delta t/\tau\) and \(y_{n}=x_{n}-I\) to obtain \(y_{n+1}=(1-\alpha )y_{n}\). The continuous deviation always decays smoothly; the discrete deviation is controlled by amplification factor \(a=1-\alpha\). Its magnitude shrinks only when \(|a|<1\).

Solving \(|1-\alpha |<1\) gives \(0<\alpha <2\). For \(0<\alpha \le 1\), the deviation keeps its sign and approaches steady state monotonically. For \(1<\alpha <2\), it alternates sign while decaying. At \(\alpha =2\), its magnitude does not shrink; for \(\alpha >2\), it grows. This is a property of the algorithm, not the biology of the original differential equation. Choose the step size relative to the system's fastest time constant.

To verify a numerical implementation, compare the Euler trajectory with a known exact solution at the same times and repeat the calculation with \(\Delta t\) and \(\Delta t/2\). Roughly halving the error is consistent with a first-order method. Also check that the first array entry is the initial value, whether an update uses \(I_{n}\) or \(I_{n+1}\), and whether time and state arrays have matching lengths. These choices matter at segment boundaries.
keyPoints: An Euler step is the current state plus the step size times the current slope.
The stability interval for first-order decay is \(0<\Delta t/\tau <2\); the monotonic interval is narrower.
Doubling or halving the step size helps separate discretization error from model behavior.

derivation.title: Derive Euler stability from the amplification factor
derivation.setup: Apply forward Euler to no-input decay \(\tau  dx/dt=-x\) and determine when every initial value converges to 0.

steps.title: Write the discrete update
steps.explanation: The derivative difference quotient gives \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}-(\Delta t/\tau )x_{n}\).

steps.title: Define the amplification factor
steps.explanation: Let \(a=1-\Delta t/\tau\). After n recursions, \(x_{n}=a^n x_{0}\).

steps.title: Require magnitude to decay
steps.explanation: For \(|x_{n}|\) to approach 0 for every finite \(x_{0}\), |a| must be less than 1.

steps.title: Solve the inequality
steps.explanation: Starting from \(-1<1-\Delta t/\tau <1\), subtract 1 and reverse signs to obtain \(0<\Delta t/\tau <2\).

symbolNotes: \(\Delta t\) is a numerical time step, not an intrinsic system parameter; \(\tau\) is the time constant of the continuous equation.
a is the dimensionless multiplier applied to the deviation on each step.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\Delta t/\tau\) is dimensionless. Both terms added in the update have the same units as x.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\Delta t\to 0\), \(a\to 1\): each change is small but the number of steps grows. At \(\Delta t=\tau\), \(a=0\) and the no-input discrete solution reaches zero in one step; that does not reproduce the intermediate continuous exponential.

workedExample.title: First four states at three step sizes
workedExample.problem: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\), \(I=0\), and \(x_{0}=1\). For \(\Delta t=5\), 15, and 25 ms, calculate the first three updates and classify the behavior.
steps: For \(\Delta t=5\), \(a=0.5\) and the sequence is 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125: monotonic decay.
For \(\Delta t=15\), \(a=-0.5\) and the sequence is 1, −0.5, 0.25, −0.125: alternating decay.
For \(\Delta t=25\), \(a=-1.5\) and the sequence is 1, −1.5, 2.25, −3.375: divergent magnitude.
The continuous system is the same positive exponential decay in all three cases; every difference comes from the numerical step size.
workedExample.result: 5 ms gives stable monotonic decay, 15 ms gives stable oscillatory decay, and 25 ms gives unstable divergence.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The three amplification-factor magnitudes are 0.5, 0.5, and 1.5, matching the observed decrease, decrease, and increase in magnitude.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does a discrete trajectory that alternates across steady state not immediately imply an oscillatory mechanism in the continuous system?
selfCheck.answer: This first-order continuous equation has only a real negative decay rate. Alternation may come from a negative Euler amplification factor. Reduce \(\Delta t\) and compare with the exact solution before calling it model dynamics rather than a numerical artifact.

pitfalls: Accepting a trajectory because the program ran without error, without checking \(\Delta t\) relative to \(\tau\).
Changing total duration or input sampling together with step size, making the error comparison uninterpretable.

modules.title: Second-order oscillator, state space, and code-boundary audit
modules.guidingQuestion: How can a system involving “acceleration” be rewritten as first-order state updates, and how can we recognize artifacts introduced by a numerical method or piecewise code?
paragraphs: The second-order equation \(d^{2}x/dt^{2}=-x\) needs both position x and velocity \(v=dx/dt\) to determine the future. Defining v gives \(dx/dt=v\) and \(dv/dt=-x\), so state \(z=(x,v)^{\mathrm{T}}\) evolves in a two-dimensional plane. For the continuous system, \(E=(x^{2}+v^{2})/2\) has derivative \(x\cdot dx/dt+v\cdot dv/dt=xv-vx=0\). The trajectory is therefore a closed curve of fixed radius, not an inward or outward spiral.

A physical oscillator must retain angular frequency \(\omega\). Under forward Euler, an energy-like quantity is multiplied by \(1+(\omega \Delta t)^{2}\) on every step. No finite \(\Delta t\) conserves it exactly, so a long simulation drifts outward. This does not mean Euler fails to converge: with total duration fixed and \(\Delta t\to 0\), cumulative amplification approaches 1 and the numerical trajectory approaches the continuous solution. Only after setting \(\omega =1\) and nondimensionalizing time can the factor be shortened to \(1+\Delta t^{2}\).

The accompanying code also simulates a first-order system with \(\tau =0.01 \mathrm{s}\), step 0.001 s, and duration 0.250 s. Inputs are 0, 2, 1, a cosine, and 0 in sequence. Each update reads the previous input \(I(t-1)\), as expected for the current-time slope in explicit Euler. The final condition is `time<0.250`, but the time vector includes the endpoint 0.250 exactly. Consequently, \(I(end)\) remains NaN and the last input point is not plotted normally.

That NaN does not immediately contaminate \(x(end)\), because the final state update reads \(I(end-1)\), not \(I(end)\). This demonstrates why “the output looks normal” does not prove that an array is complete. A second semantic error concerns \(t_{0}=0.150\) in \(\cos(\omega (t-t_{0}))\): this is a phase-reference time, so a comment calling it a frequency conflicts with its units. The actual frequency parameter is angular frequency \(\omega =220 \mathrm{rad}/s\). Audit comments, formulas, units, and indices together.
keyPoints: A second-order system can be represented by two coupled first-order equations for position and velocity.
Forward Euler multiplies an undamped oscillator's energy-like quantity by \(1+(\omega \Delta t)^{2}\) each step; only the nondimensional \(\omega =1\) form becomes \(1+\Delta t^{2}\).
Array endpoints, strict inequalities, and use of a previous index jointly determine whether NaN propagates.

derivation.title: Prove the finite-step energy drift of forward Euler
derivation.setup: Apply step h to \(dx/dt=v\) and \(dv/dt=-\omega ^{2}x\). Define twice the energy-like quantity as \(2E=v^{2}+\omega ^{2}x^{2}\) and compare E before and after one Euler step.

steps.title: Write both updates
steps.explanation: Advance position along the current velocity and change velocity along the current restoring acceleration.

steps.title: Expand the updated energy
steps.explanation: Expand \(v_{n+1}^{2}\) and \(\omega ^{2}x_{n+1}^{2}\) separately; their cross terms have equal magnitude and opposite sign.

steps.title: Cancel the cross terms
steps.explanation: Adding the expansions leaves the original energy multiplied by a factor strictly greater than 1.

steps.title: Accumulate the finite-step error
steps.explanation: With total duration \(T=nh\), the energy ratio after n repetitions is the expression below. Every fixed \(h>0\) produces outward drift.

steps.title: Check the convergence limit
steps.explanation: At fixed T, let \(h\to 0\). The logarithm of the ratio is approximately \(T\omega ^{2}h\) and approaches 0, so the energy ratio approaches 1. Euler is not conservative, but it still converges on a finite time interval.

symbolNotes: \(\omega\) is angular frequency with units of inverse time. The simplified equation \(dv/dt=-x\) corresponds to \(\omega =1\) in nondimensional time.
h is the numerical step and T is the fixed total duration used for comparison. A statement about energy drift must specify both.
derivation.unitsCheck: hv has the same units as x, \(h\omega ^{2}x\) has the same units as v, and \(\omega h\) is dimensionless. Because \(v^{2}\) and \(\omega ^{2}x^{2}\) share units, they can form one energy-like quantity.
derivation.limitCheck: For every finite \(h>0\), the per-step factor exceeds 1. At fixed T with \(h\to 0\), the cumulative factor approaches 1. If T grows as 1/h or faster, long-time structural error may remain substantial.

workedExample.title: Locate an endpoint bug in a piecewise input
workedExample.problem: The time vector is 0:0.001:0.250. The last input branch assigns 0 only when \(t<0.250\); all other values remain preallocated as NaN. How many time points exist, which one is NaN, and does it enter the final x update?
steps: From 0 to 0.250 in increments of 0.001 gives \(0.250/0.001+1=251\) points.
The final point \(t=0.250\) fails the strict inequality \(t<0.250\), so \(I(251)\) remains NaN.
If the loop computes \(x(k)\) from \(I(k-1)\), then \(x(251)\) reads \(I(250)\), which corresponds to \(t=0.249\) and equals 0.
Thus \(x(251)\) remains finite in the current loop, but the input plot lacks its last point. Any later read of \(I(251)\) would propagate NaN.
workedExample.result: There are 251 points, and \(I(251)\) is NaN. It does not enter the final explicit update here, but it exposes a gap in the boundary conditions.
workedExample.sanityCheck: An interval of length 0.250 s contains 250 steps of this size, so it must contain 1 more endpoint than steps.

selfCheck.prompt: What two checks, at minimum, distinguish an outward spiral caused by the continuous model from one caused by the numerical method?
selfCheck.answer: First calculate a continuous invariant such as the energy derivative, or the system's eigenvalues. Then vary the step size and compare with an energy-preserving method or an exact solution. If continuous energy is constant while Euler energy grows, the artifact is localized.

pitfalls: Interpreting a spiral in a phase portrait as damping or self-excitation before checking the discrete update matrix.
Trusting variable comments without checking how the variable appears in equations and what units it carries.
Missing the final array assignment because the time vector includes the right endpoint while the branch uses a strict inequality.

objectives: Build a consistent sign convention from the definitions of force, potential energy, electric potential, and membrane voltage, and explain how a concentration gradient and an electric field jointly determine net ionic flux.
Derive the Nernst equation from the electrochemical equilibrium of a single ion, handling the valence z, the inside-to-outside concentration ratio, temperature, and voltage sign correctly.
Map the lipid membrane, ion channels, and applied current onto a capacitor, conductance–battery branches, and a current source, then derive the membrane equation from charge conservation.
Distinguish the perfect integrate-and-fire model from the leaky integrate-and-fire model, and calculate their slopes, time constants, steady-state voltages, rheobase currents, and first-spike times.
State what the equivalent circuit, integrate-and-fire model, and action-potential mechanism each retain and omit, without interpreting model components as literal biological parts.
prerequisiteBridge: Electric charge may be positive or negative, and Coulomb force has both magnitude and direction. Potential energy U measures a system's capacity to do work at a position, with \(F=-\nabla U\); the minus sign means that the force points toward decreasing potential energy. Electric potential \(\phi =U/q\) is potential energy per unit charge, so the same potential difference produces opposite energy changes \(q\Delta \phi\) for positive and negative ions. Throughout this lecture, membrane voltage is defined as \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\): if the intracellular potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential, \(V_{m}=-60 \mathrm{mV}\). Begin every directional argument from this definition.

Diffusion arises from thermal motion in a nonuniform concentration: net particle flux runs from higher to lower concentration. If a membrane is permeable to only one ionic species, movement of a small number of ions separates charge across the membrane and creates an opposing electric field. At equilibrium, the chemical and electrical driving forces balance, so macroscopic net flux is zero even though individual ions continue to move in both directions. A logarithm converts a concentration ratio into an energy difference; an exponential converts that energy difference back into a concentration or probability ratio.

Only four circuit ideas are needed to begin: voltage is a difference in electric potential, current is the rate of charge flow \(I=dQ/dt\), a capacitor obeys \(Q=CV\), and a resistive branch can be written \(I=G(V-E)\), where \(G=1/R\). Unit conversion is crucial: \(1 \mathrm{pA}/1 \mathrm{pF}=1 \mathrm{V}/s\), and \(1 \mathrm{V}/s=1 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\). The positive current direction must be declared. Here, inward depolarizing current \(I_{e}\) enters the right-hand side positively, whereas outward ionic current \(G(V-E)\), which removes charge from the membrane capacitor, is subtracted.

The first-order time-constant analysis from the previous lecture applies directly. For \(\tau  dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), voltage approaches \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) exponentially from its initial value. A threshold–reset rule adds discrete events to that continuous trajectory. Understand the continuous voltage evolution and discrete spike events separately before combining them. The model does not reproduce an action-potential waveform; it represents a spike by the threshold-crossing time, an abstraction suited to studying spike timing and firing rate.

diagnostic.prompt: If \(V_{m}=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\), which side has the lower electric potential? On which side does a cation have lower electric potential energy?
diagnostic.answer: The intracellular electric potential is 60 mV below the extracellular potential. For a cation with \(q>0\), \(U=q\phi\), so its electric potential energy is also lower inside.
diagnostic.explanation: First use the voltage definition to order the electric potentials, then multiply by the sign of the charge to order potential energies. The ordering reverses for anions, so “negative inside” alone cannot determine the direction of every ion.

diagnostic.prompt: Intracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration exceeds extracellular \(K^{+}\) concentration, and the Nernst equation uses \(\ln([K]_{\mathrm{out}}/[K]_{\mathrm{in}})\). Is the equilibrium potential positive or negative?
diagnostic.answer: Because \(z=+1\) and the concentration ratio is less than 1, the logarithm is negative; therefore \(E_{K}\) is negative.
diagnostic.explanation: The \(K^{+}\) concentration gradient drives efflux. Preventing net efflux requires a negative intracellular potential that attracts \(K^{+}\) inward, so the inside-minus-outside equilibrium potential is negative.

diagnostic.prompt: A membrane capacitor has \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\) and receives a constant inward current of 100 pA. Ignoring all ion channels, what is \(dV/dt\)?
diagnostic.answer: \(dV/dt=I/C=0.5 \mathrm{V}/s=0.5 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\).
diagnostic.explanation: The \(10^{-12}\) factors in pA/pF cancel to give V/s, whose numerical value equals mV/ms. A constant current therefore produces a linear voltage ramp across an ideal capacitor.

diagnostic.prompt: In a leaky integrate-and-fire model, \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). What minimum constant current places the subthreshold steady state exactly at threshold?
diagnostic.answer: \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})=10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot 15 \mathrm{mV}=150 \mathrm{pA}\).
diagnostic.explanation: At threshold, \(dV/dt=0\) requires the applied current to exactly balance the leak current. Because \(\mathrm{nS}\cdot \mathrm{mV}=\mathrm{pA}\), any smaller current leaves the steady state below threshold.

modules.title: Electrochemical potential, membrane voltage, and Nernst equilibrium
modules.guidingQuestion: When an ion moves across a membrane down its concentration gradient, how does charge separation create an opposing electric field, and at what voltage does net flux vanish?
paragraphs: The cell membrane separates two conducting saline solutions. Most of the fluid on either side remains nearly electroneutral: membrane voltage requires only a tiny fraction of ions to separate at the membrane surfaces, not a cell interior filled with negative charge. Use \(F=-\nabla U\) and \(\phi =U/q\), and define \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\). A resting value near −60 mV means that the intracellular potential is lower. The same convention governs reversal potentials, channel currents, and action-potential diagrams.

A concentration gradient supplies the diffusive drive. Suppose only \(K^{+}\) channels are open and \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}>[K]_{\mathrm{out}}\). Random motion produces net \(K^{+}\) efflux and leaves the inside relatively negative. As charge separation grows, the negative intracellular potential attracts \(K^{+}\) back inward. The chemical drive remains outward while the electrical drive points inward. At equilibrium, their contributions to the electrochemical-potential difference cancel, yielding zero net flux—not an end to microscopic ion exchange.

For a dilute solution, the molar electrochemical potential of an ion is \(\mu =\mu ^{0}+RT \ln c+zF\phi\). This is equivalent to the single-particle Boltzmann form in the source: \(q_{c}=z e\), \(R=N_{Ak,B}\), and \(F=N_{Ae}\), so \(RT/(zF)=k_{\mathrm{BT}}/q_{c}\). At equilibrium, \(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}}=\exp(q_{c}E/k_{\mathrm{BT}})\); taking the logarithm gives \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_{\mathrm{out}}=(RT/zF)\ln(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}})\). For a cation, \(z>0\) preserves the logarithm's sign. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses it.

An equilibrium potential is not the voltage that a membrane must have at every instant. It is the voltage at which the net current carried by one ionic species is zero. Away from \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\), current direction depends on the driving force \(V_{m}-E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) together with channel conductance. Values of about +55 mV for \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), −75 mV for \(K^{+}\), +125 mV for \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), and −60 mV for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) are illustrative rather than universal. Nernst potentials vary with concentration, temperature, and activity, while the actual \(V_{m}\) depends on multiple permeabilities and dynamic gating.

This framework also explains the direction of an action-potential trajectory. Rapid Na⁺-channel opening pulls \(V_{m}\) toward the positive \(E_{\mathrm{Na}}\). \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) inactivation and a delayed rise in \(K^{+}\) conductance then pull \(V_{m}\) back toward \(E_{K}\), after which channel recovery and leak currents return the membrane to rest. Approaching a reversal potential does not instantaneously equalize ion concentrations: only a small fraction of the cellular ion reservoir crosses the membrane during one action potential.
keyPoints: Membrane voltage arises from a small separation of charge at the membrane surfaces; the bulk intracellular and extracellular solutions remain nearly electroneutral.
Nernst equilibrium is a zero-net-flux state in which chemical and electrical driving forces cancel.
The sign of \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) is set jointly by the definition \(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_{\mathrm{out}}\), the concentration ratio, and the signed valence z.
A reversal potential is the zero-current voltage for one ionic branch, not the membrane voltage at every instant.

derivation.title: From a single-ion Boltzmann ratio to the Nernst equation
derivation.setup: Assume that the membrane is permeable to a single ionic species with charge \(q_{c}=z e\), that temperature T is constant, and that the solutions on both sides are approximately ideal and dilute. At equilibrium, the electrochemical occupancies are compatible and net transmembrane flux is zero.

steps.title: Write the Boltzmann weight
steps.explanation: The probability of a state decreases exponentially with its potential energy; the electric potential energy of one ion is its charge times the local electric potential.

steps.title: Relate the occupancy ratio to the concentration ratio
steps.explanation: The equilibrium occupancy of the same ion on the two sides is represented by their concentration ratio, with the transmembrane potential difference entering the exponent.

steps.title: Write the electrochemical potential on each side
steps.explanation: The two sides have \(\mu _{\mathrm{in}}=\mu ^{0}+RT \ln c_{\mathrm{in}}+zF\phi _{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(\mu _{\mathrm{out}}=\mu ^{0}+RT \ln c_{\mathrm{out}}+zF\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\), respectively.

steps.title: Connect single-particle and molar notation
steps.explanation: Using \(q_{c}=z e\), \(R=N_{Ak,B}\), and \(F=N_{Ae}\), divide molar energy by Avogadro's constant to obtain \(RT/(zF)=k_{\mathrm{BT}}/q_{c}\). Thus, the Boltzmann concentration ratio and the molar Nernst equation express the same physical equilibrium in two unit systems.

steps.title: Impose electrochemical equilibrium
steps.explanation: Zero net flux corresponds to \(\mu _{\mathrm{in}}=\mu _{\mathrm{out}}\). The standard chemical potential \(\mu ^{0}\) is identical for the same ion on both sides, so rearrangement gives \(zF(\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}})=RT \ln(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}})\).

steps.title: Insert the membrane-voltage definition
steps.explanation: Use \(V_{m}=\phi _{\mathrm{in}}-\phi _{\mathrm{out}}\) and denote the equilibrium membrane voltage for this ion by \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\).

steps.title: Solve for the equilibrium potential
steps.explanation: Dividing by zF yields \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=(RT/zF)\ln(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}})\). Because valence appears in the denominator, a divalent ion has half the voltage magnitude of a monovalent ion at the same concentration ratio.

steps.title: Connect the result to current direction
steps.explanation: Under a linear conductance approximation, \(I_{\mathrm{ion}}=G_{\mathrm{ion}}(V_{m}-E_{\mathrm{ion}})\). Current through this branch is zero at \(V_{m}=E_{\mathrm{ion}}\); away from that voltage, the sign gives the direction under the stated convention.

symbolNotes: \(N_{A}\) is Avogadro's constant, and e is the positive magnitude of the elementary charge. The signed valence z carries the sign of ionic charge, so \(q_{c}=z e\).
\(k_{B}\) and \(q_{c}\) are per-particle quantities; R and F are per-mole quantities. Do not mix the two notation systems.

\(c_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{out}}\) are the intracellular and extracellular activities, or approximate concentrations, of the same ion. They must use the same units so that their ratio is dimensionless.
The valence z includes its sign: +1 for \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\) and \(K^{+}\), +2 for \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), and −1 for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\).
\(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) uses inside potential minus outside potential. Reversing the voltage definition reverses the overall sign of the formula.
derivation.unitsCheck: RT has units J/mol and F has units C/mol, so \(RT/F=J/C=V\). The concentration ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless; \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) is measured in volts.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(c_{\mathrm{out}}=c_{\mathrm{in}}\), the logarithm is zero and \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}=0\). Increasing \(c_{\mathrm{out}}/c_{\mathrm{in}}\) for a cation makes \(E_{\mathrm{ion}}\) more positive. The ideal formula tends toward zero voltage as \(T\to 0\), but a physiological model is not valid at absolute zero.

workedExample.title: Calculate the \(K^{+}\) equilibrium potential at body temperature
workedExample.problem: Use \(T=310 K\), so \(RT/F\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\); for \(K^{+}\), let \([K]_{\mathrm{out}}=5 \mathrm{mM}\), \([K]_{\mathrm{in}}=140 \mathrm{mM}\), and \(z=+1\). Calculate \(E_{K}\), then determine how it changes when extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises to 10 mM.
steps: The initial concentration ratio is \(5/140\approx 0.035714\), and \(\ln(0.035714)\approx -3.332\).
\(E_{K}\approx 26.7 \mathrm{mV}\cdot (-3.332)=-88.96 \mathrm{mV}\), or about −89 mV.
After extracellular \(K^{+}\) rises, the ratio is \(10/140\approx 0.071429\) and its logarithm is ≈−2.639.
The new value is \(E_{K}\approx 26.7\cdot (-2.639)=-70.46 \mathrm{mV}\), about 18.5 mV more positive than before—a depolarizing shift.
workedExample.result: Initially \(E_{K}\approx -89 \mathrm{mV}\); doubling extracellular \(K^{+}\) shifts \(E_{K}\) to ≈−70.5 mV.
workedExample.sanityCheck: In both cases \(c_{\mathrm{out}}<c_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(z>0\), so \(E_{K}\) must be negative. Raising the external concentration moves the ratio toward 1 and reduces the magnitude of the potential.
