selfCheck.prompt: If \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) had the same inside-to-outside concentration ratio, why would its equilibrium potential have the opposite sign from that of \(K^{+}\)?
selfCheck.answer: In the Nernst equation, signed valence z appears in the denominator. For \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), \(z=-1\) reverses the sign of the logarithmic term, reflecting the reversal of electric force for a negative charge.

pitfalls: Mixing \([ion]_{\mathrm{in}}/[ion]_{\mathrm{out}}\) with \([ion]_{\mathrm{out}}/[ion]_{\mathrm{in}}\) without changing the sign to match the voltage convention.
Using \(z=+1\) for \(\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) and thereby obtaining an equilibrium potential with the wrong sign.
Interpreting zero net flux as no microscopic exchange, or interpreting a reversal potential as equal concentrations.

modules.title: The membrane equivalent circuit: capacitance, conductance, batteries, and KCL
modules.guidingQuestion: How does each biological membrane feature map onto a circuit element, and how does charge conservation combine those elements into a membrane-voltage equation?
paragraphs: The lipid bilayer separates conducting solutions and allows opposite charges to accumulate on its inner and outer surfaces, so it acts as a capacitor C. Ion channels provide selective conducting pathways; the number of open channels and their single-channel conductance combine into a conductance G. Each ion's concentration gradient sets a reversal potential E, represented by a battery in series with the conductance. An external electrode or synaptic input injects charge and is represented by a current source \(I_{e}\). This equivalent circuit preserves relationships among charge flow and voltage; it does not claim that the membrane contains metal components.

For fixed C, \(Q=CV\) means that changing voltage requires changing surface charge. Differentiating gives \(dQ/dt=C dV/dt\), and the definition \(I=dQ/dt\) therefore gives \(I_{C}=C dV/dt\). Injecting 100 pA into a 200 pF capacitor produces a slope of 0.5 mV/ms. A capacitor alone does not set a steady state: as long as a nonzero constant net current persists, voltage continues to change linearly.

Under a linear conductance approximation, an ionic branch obeys \(I_{x}=G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\). Net current is zero at \(V_{m}=E_{x}\), and the driving force grows with the distance from \(E_{x}\). \(G_{x}\) may be constant, as for a passive leak \(G_{L}\), or vary with voltage and time, as do \(G_{\mathrm{Na}}(t,V)\) and \(G_{K}(t,V)\) in the Hodgkin–Huxley model. The battery \(E_{x}\) sets the zero-current voltage; conductance determines the current produced by a given driving force.

Apply Kirchhoff's current law at the membrane node: net current entering the capacitor equals applied current minus the outward ionic currents, giving C \(dV_{m}/dt=I_{e}-\sum _x G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\). Every term has units of current. A positive net sum deposits positive charge on the inner capacitor plate and raises \(V_{m}\); a negative sum lowers \(V_{m}\); a zero sum makes voltage momentarily stationary. This equation is the common backbone of the IF, LIF, and Hodgkin–Huxley models.

The Hodgkin–Huxley equivalent circuit contains the membrane capacitor, a leak branch, and variable Na and K branches. Conductance changes during an action potential make those branches compete: increasing \(G_{\mathrm{Na}}\) pulls V more strongly toward \(E_{\mathrm{Na}}\), whereas increasing \(G_{K}\) pulls V toward \(E_{K}\). “Pull toward” does not mean setting voltage instantaneously to a reversal potential; capacitance and every other open branch determine the rate and trajectory.
keyPoints: The lipid membrane maps to capacitance, ion channels to conductance, and concentration gradients to reversal-potential batteries.
\(I_{C}=C dV/dt\) follows from \(Q=CV\) and \(I=dQ/dt\).
KCL combines applied current and all ionic branches into one voltage-dynamics equation.
Conductance sets the strength of attraction toward a reversal potential; capacitance sets how quickly voltage can change.

derivation.title: Derive the multichannel membrane equation from charge conservation
derivation.setup: The membrane has capacitance C, receives an applied current \(I_{e}\) defined as positive inward, and contains several ionic branches. Define branch current from inside to outside as \(I_{x}=G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\).

steps.title: Relate charge to voltage
steps.explanation: The relative charge on the inner membrane surface is \(Q=C V_{m}\). Assuming that C is constant, \(dQ/dt=C dV_{m}/dt\).

steps.title: Write conservation at the node
steps.explanation: The rate of increase of intracellular surface charge equals inward applied current \(I_{e}\) minus all branch currents flowing from inside to outside.

steps.title: Substitute the conductance branches
steps.explanation: Using \(I_{x}=G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\) gives C \(dV_{m}/dt=I_{e}-\sum _x G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\).

steps.title: Solve the constant-conductance steady state
steps.explanation: If every \(G_{x}\) is constant, set \(dV/dt=0\) and rearrange to obtain \(V^{*}= [I_{e}+\sum _x G_{x} E_{x}]/\sum _x G_{x}\): a conductance-weighted reversal potential plus the offset caused by applied current.

steps.title: Identify the time scale
steps.explanation: With total conductance \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum G_{x}\), write the equation as \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V^{*}\), where \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\). Opening more channels therefore shortens the time constant.

symbolNotes: By convention, positive \(I_{e}\) injects positive charge into the cell, while positive \(I_{x}\) carries positive charge from inside to outside.
\(G_{x}\ge 0\) is branch conductance and \(E_{x}\) is that ion's reversal potential; \(G_{x}(V-E_{x})\) may be positive or negative.
C is total membrane capacitance. If parameters are expressed per unit area, divide every term in the equation by membrane area.
derivation.unitsCheck: C·dV/dt has units \(F\cdot V/s=C/s=A\), and G·(V−E) has units \(S\cdot V=A\), so every term can be added in one KCL equation.
derivation.limitCheck: If all \(G_{x}=0\), the equation reduces to the ideal capacitor \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no finite steady state. If one \(G_{k}\) greatly exceeds all other conductances while \(I_{e}\) remains finite, \(V^{*}\) approaches \(E_{k}\).

workedExample.title: Instantaneous slope and steady state of a two-branch membrane
workedExample.problem: Use \(E_{K}=-85 \mathrm{mV}\) as the specified branch parameter for this independent circuit example; it need not equal the −89 mV obtained from a different concentration set above. Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{K}=20 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(I_{e}=300 \mathrm{pA}\). Find \(dV/dt\) at \(V=-60 \mathrm{mV}\) and the steady state \(V^{*}\).
steps: The outward leak current is \(10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-60+65)\mathrm{mV}=50 \mathrm{pA}\).
The outward K current is \(20 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-60+85)\mathrm{mV}=500 \mathrm{pA}\), so net inward current is \(300-50-500=-250 \mathrm{pA}\).
Thus \(dV/dt=-250 \mathrm{pA}/200 \mathrm{pF}=-1.25 \mathrm{V}/s=-1.25 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\), so voltage is falling at this instant.
The steady-state numerator is \(300 \mathrm{pA}+10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-65 \mathrm{mV})+20 \mathrm{nS}\cdot (-85 \mathrm{mV})=300-650-1700=-2050 \mathrm{pA}\).
Total conductance is 30 nS, so \(V^{*}=-2050/30 \mathrm{mV}\approx -68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) and \(\tau =C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}=200 \mathrm{pF}/30 \mathrm{nS}\approx 6.67 \mathrm{ms}\).
workedExample.result: At −60 mV, \(dV/dt=-1.25 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms}\); the steady state is approximately −68.3 mV and the time constant is approximately 6.67 ms.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The steady state should reflect competition among the two branches after the current-induced shift. Substituting \(V=-68.33 \mathrm{mV}\) makes the total outward branch current approximately 300 pA.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does increasing one channel conductance change both the steady-state voltage and the speed of approach?
selfCheck.answer: It gives that channel's reversal potential more weight in the steady-state average and increases \(G_{\mathrm{tot}}\), which reduces the membrane time constant \(C/G_{\mathrm{tot}}\); voltage therefore approaches the new steady state faster.

pitfalls: Memorizing C dV/dt without declaring current directions, then mixing sign conventions across ionic branches.
Treating reversal potential E as if conductance created it. E comes from an electrochemical gradient; G sets current magnitude.
Forgetting that \(\mathrm{nS}\cdot \mathrm{mV}=\mathrm{pA}\), or reporting pA/pF as mV/s instead of V/s or mV/ms.

modules.title: From perfect integrate-and-fire to leaky integrate-and-fire
modules.guidingQuestion: What firing behavior follows from threshold and reset alone, and why does adding a leak branch create a steady state, a rheobase current, and a nonlinear F–I curve?
paragraphs: The perfect integrate-and-fire model retains capacitance C and applied current \(I_{e}\), with subthreshold equation \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\). A constant positive current produces a linear ramp with slope \(I_{e}/C\). When V reaches threshold \(V_{T}\), the model records a spike and resets V to \(V_{R}\). Spike times stand in for action potentials; the model does not reproduce waveforms generated by Na and K conductances. It converts input current into interspike intervals but has no resting attractor.

Moving from \(V_{R}\) to \(V_{T}\) requires \(\Delta V=V_{T}-V_{R}\). Under constant current, the ramp time is \(\Delta t=C\Delta V/I_{e}\), so without a refractory period \(f=1/\Delta t=I_{e}/[C(V_{T}-V_{R})]\). Every \(I_{e}>0\) eventually produces a spike, so the perfect model has no positive rheobase current and its F–I curve rises linearly from the origin. Real neurons, by contrast, may remain at rest under a weak constant input.

Adding a leak branch gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Leak grows with the displacement of V from \(E_{L}\) and always pulls voltage toward \(E_{L}\). With \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\), the equation becomes \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Under constant input, \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\); voltage approaches a finite steady state exponentially instead of rising without bound.

Spiking requires \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) to lie above threshold. The boundary condition \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=V_{T}\) gives \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). If \(I_{e}\le I_{T}\), the steady state remains subthreshold and sustained current produces no periodic spikes. If \(I_{e}>I_{T}\), the exponential solution gives the travel time from \(V_{R}\) to \(V_{T}\). This threshold current emerges from the balance between input and leak; it is not an extra current rule inserted by hand.

LIF still omits the action-potential waveform, channel gating, adaptation, and absolute refractoriness, but it links biophysical circuit elements to spike events. Compare models term by term: perfect IF and LIF both contain capacitance, threshold, and reset; only LIF contains \(E_{L}\), \(G_{L}\), a finite steady state, and a positive rheobase. Identifying the responsible term lets you interpret an F–I change as a mechanistic consequence.
keyPoints: Perfect IF ramps linearly under constant current; every positive current eventually produces a spike.
The leak branch introduces \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\).
The LIF rheobase current is \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\).
Threshold and reset are event rules, not a simulation of the action-potential waveform.

derivation.title: LIF steady state, rheobase, and first-spike time
derivation.setup: Consider \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\) with constant \(I_{e}\), initial voltage \(V(0)=V_{R}\), and threshold \(V_{T}>V_{R}\).

steps.title: Define the time constant and steady state
steps.explanation: Rewrite the right-hand side as \(-G_{L}[V-(E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L})]\), then define \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\).

steps.title: Write the subthreshold solution
steps.explanation: This is a first-order linear system with steady state \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), so \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{R}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})\exp(-t/\tau _{m})\).

steps.title: Obtain the rheobase current
steps.explanation: A trajectory starting below threshold can cross only if \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\). The boundary \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=V_{T}\) gives \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\).

steps.title: Solve for the threshold-crossing time
steps.explanation: Set \(V(t_{sp})=V_{T}\) and rearrange to obtain \(\exp(-t_{sp}/\tau _{m})=(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})\).

steps.title: Take the logarithm
steps.explanation: When \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}>V_{R}\), the ratio lies between 0 and 1, giving \(t_{sp}=\tau _{m} \ln[(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})]\). Without a refractory period, the periodic firing rate is \(1/t_{sp}\).

symbolNotes: \(V_{R}\) is the reset voltage after each spike and \(V_{T}\) is the event threshold; neither is an ionic reversal potential.
\(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) is the constant-input steady state of the subthreshold equation when reset is disabled.
\(\tau _{m}\) is capacitance divided by leak conductance. Increasing capacitance slows the response; increasing conductance speeds it up.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(C/G_{L}\) has units \(F/S=s\); \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) has units \(A/S=V\); the logarithm contains a dimensionless ratio of voltage differences; \(t_{sp}\) is a time.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(I_{e}\) approaches \(I_{T}\) from above, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T}\to 0\), \(t_{sp}\to \infty\), and firing \(\mathrm{rate}\to 0\). For very large \(I_{e}\), leak matters less during the short ramp and the result approaches the perfect-IF value \(C(V_{T}-V_{R})/I_{e}\).

workedExample.title: Compare subthreshold behavior and repetitive firing with the same parameters
workedExample.problem: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\). Apply constant currents of 100 pA and 200 pA. Determine whether each causes spiking; if so, calculate the first-spike time and the rate without a refractory period.
steps: The membrane time constant is \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}=200 \mathrm{pF}/10 \mathrm{nS}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), and the rheobase is \(I_{T}=10 \mathrm{nS}\cdot 15 \mathrm{mV}=150 \mathrm{pA}\).
At 100 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65 \mathrm{mV}+100 \mathrm{pA}/10 \mathrm{nS}=-55 \mathrm{mV}\), below −50 mV, so the trajectory never crosses threshold.
At 200 pA, \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65+20=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), above threshold. The threshold-time ratio is \((V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})=20/5=4\).
Therefore \(t_{sp}=20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot \ln 4\approx 20\cdot 1.3863=27.73 \mathrm{ms}\). Each reset returns to the same voltage under the same input, so every cycle has the same duration.
Without a refractory period, \(f=1/0.02773 \mathrm{s}\approx 36.1 \mathrm{Hz}\).
workedExample.result: At 100 pA, voltage approaches −55 mV without spiking. At 200 pA, the first interval is about 27.7 ms and the repetitive rate is about 36.1 Hz.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Because 200 pA is only slightly above the 150 pA rheobase, the rate should be finite and modest. Ignoring leak, perfect IF gives \(15 \mathrm{mV}/(1 \mathrm{mV}/\mathrm{ms})=15 \mathrm{ms}\), correctly predicting a faster crossing.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does 100 pA eventually produce a spike in perfect IF but never produce one in the LIF model above?
selfCheck.answer: Perfect IF has no opposing leak, so positive current continues to charge the capacitor. In LIF, leak grows during depolarization until it exactly balances 100 pA at −55 mV, a steady state below the −50 mV threshold.

pitfalls: Treating \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) as the voltage immediately after reset, or treating threshold \(V_{T}\) as a reversal potential.
Applying the logarithmic crossing-time formula when \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\le V_{T}\) and assigning physical meaning to the resulting number.
Mistaking the model's zero-width spike event for the voltage waveform of a biological action potential.

objectives: Rewrite the LIF equation in time-constant–steady-state form and explain the exponential trajectory after a current step begins and ends.
Derive the exact interspike interval and F–I curve of the LIF model from the threshold condition, and analyze behavior near rheobase and in the strong-input limit.
Interpret current direction and maximal conductance in the leak, \(\mathrm{Na}^{+}\), and \(K^{+}\) branches of the Hodgkin–Huxley membrane equation.
Derive a gating variable's steady state and time constant from the transition rates of a two-state channel, and explain activation, inactivation, and refractoriness.

Explain how area normalization, multicompartment propagation, and cellular diversity extend a point-neuron model without confusing passive subthreshold decay with active action-potential regeneration.
prerequisiteBridge: Begin with the circuit convention from the previous lecture: \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Capacitance sets how rapidly voltage changes under a given net current; leak conductance pulls voltage toward \(E_{L}\). Divide by \(G_{L}\): \(C/G_{L}\) has units of time, whereas \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) has units of voltage. These combinations define \(\tau _{m}\) and the input-driven shift in steady state. If the units fail, the subsequent exponential solution and F–I relationship have no physical meaning.

Solving a threshold-crossing time uses the inverse relationship between the exponential and natural logarithm. If \(e^{-t/\tau }=a\) with \(0<a<1\), then \(-t/\tau =\ln a\). Because \(\ln a<0\), \(t=-\tau  \ln a\) is positive. A logarithm's argument must be dimensionless, so the formula contains a ratio of two voltage differences. Near the critical input, this ratio approaches 0 and the logarithm diverges, meaning that the first threshold crossing takes very long.

First interpret a Hodgkin–Huxley gating variable as the fraction of many independent gates in the open state, so m, h, and n lie between 0 and 1. If a channel requires three m gates and one h gate to be open simultaneously, the independence approximation gives open fraction \(m^{3}h\). These exponents are not arbitrary decorations for fitting: they arise from the joint probability that several gates meet their conditions together. Multiplying maximal conductance by the open fraction gives instantaneous conductance.

A spatial model must distinguish total quantities from quantities per unit area. Total capacitance scales with membrane area A as \(C=c_{m} A\), and total conductance as \(G=gA\). Dividing the membrane equation by A gives current density and area-specific parameters, allowing cells of different sizes to be compared. Passive subthreshold voltage decays along an axon because of leak, whereas an action potential recruits voltage-gated conductances in adjacent membrane segments and is regenerated over long distances.

diagnostic.prompt: For \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\) and \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), what is \(\tau _{m}\)? If C doubles while \(G_{L}\) remains fixed, how does the trajectory change?
diagnostic.answer: \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}=20 \mathrm{ms}\). Doubling C gives \(\tau _{m}=40 \mathrm{ms}\); the steady state is unchanged, but the trajectory approaches it more slowly.
diagnostic.explanation: Current and conductance set the steady state; capacitance appears only in the time constant. Separating steady-state location from approach speed is central to reading a first-order membrane equation.

diagnostic.prompt: Why does the LIF firing rate rise gradually from zero when \(I_{e}\) barely exceeds \(I_{T}\) instead of jumping to a high value?
diagnostic.answer: \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) then lies only slightly above \(V_{T}\). The exponential trajectory moves very slowly as it nears steady state, the logarithmic threshold time diverges, and firing frequency approaches zero.
diagnostic.explanation: Although threshold is a discrete event, continuous dynamics before the event determine its waiting time. Critical slowing creates the nonlinear onset of the F–I curve.

diagnostic.prompt: A gating variable obeys \(dn/dt=\alpha (1-n)-\beta n\). What are its steady state and time constant?
diagnostic.answer: \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\) and \(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\); equivalently, \(\tau _{n} dn/dt=-n+n_{\mathrm{inf}}\).
diagnostic.explanation: \(\alpha\) moves closed gates toward the open state, whereas \(\beta\) moves open gates toward the closed state. Their sum sets relaxation speed, and their ratio sets the steady-state open probability.

diagnostic.prompt: n rises from 0.3 to 0.6 while the K-channel open fraction is \(n^{4}\). By what factor does the open fraction increase?
diagnostic.explanation: The gating variable itself only doubles, but requiring multiple gates to open together raises the change to the fourth power, producing a steep voltage dependence of conductance.

modules.title: LIF time constant, steady state, and current-step response
modules.guidingQuestion: How do capacitance and leak convert a constant current into an exponential voltage response, and why does voltage return to rest with the same time constant after the step ends?
paragraphs: The first two pages rebuild the circuit from an ideal capacitor to a leaky integrate-and-fire membrane. An ideal capacitor obeys \(C dV/dt=I_{e}\) and has no steady state under constant current. Adding leak gives \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\). Above \(E_{L}\), outward leak current is positive and opposes further depolarization; below \(E_{L}\), current reverses and drives voltage upward. Thus \(E_{L}\) is the stable point with no input.

Define \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\) to write \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-V+V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Under constant current, \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\). The solution contains its final target \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) and an initial deviation that decays over time. After one \(\tau _{m}\), 36.8% of the deviation remains; after three \(\tau _{m}\), about 5% remains.

At current-step onset, voltage cannot jump: a finite current cannot change the finite charge on a capacitor instantaneously. The initial slope is \([I_{e}-G_{L}(V_{0}-E_{L})]/C\). Starting from \(V_{0}=E_{L}\) makes initial leak zero and slope \(I_{e}/C\). As V rises, leak grows, net current falls, and the trajectory flattens. This curvature is the direct signature of competition between capacitive charging and leak.

After the step ends at \(t_{\mathrm{off}}\), input becomes zero and the new steady state changes immediately to \(E_{L}\). Voltage itself remains continuous and takes its value at step offset as the new initial value, then decays as \(V(t)=E_{L}+[V(t_{\mathrm{off}})-E_{L}]e^{-(t-t_off)/\tau _{m}}\). Rise and recovery use the same \(\tau _{m}\) because C and \(G_{L}\) have not changed. Different experimental time constants imply at least one voltage-dependent conductance or changing parameter.
keyPoints: \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) controls speed, while \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\) sets the steady state under constant current.
Capacitor voltage is continuous; a current step changes its slope immediately, not its value.
With fixed C and \(G_{L}\), the onset and offset exponentials share one time constant.

derivation.title: Convert the leaky-membrane equation to standard first-order form
derivation.setup: Solve \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})\) under constant \(I_{e}\) with initial value \(V(0)=V_{0}\).

steps.title: Collect the voltage terms
steps.explanation: Write the right-hand side as \(-G_{L} V+G_{L}\) \(E_{L}+I_{e}=-G_{L}[V-(E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L})]\).

steps.title: Define composite parameters
steps.explanation: Let \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\). Dividing by \(G_{L}\) gives \(\tau _{m} dV/dt=-(V-V_{\mathrm{inf}})\).

steps.title: Solve for the deviation
steps.explanation: Set \(y=V-V_{\mathrm{inf}}\). Then \(\tau _{m} dy/dt=-y\) and \(y(t)=y(0)e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\).

steps.title: Recover voltage
steps.explanation: Because \(y(0)=V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{0}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\).

symbolNotes: \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) is the subthreshold steady state obtained when threshold and reset are disabled.
\(\tau _{m}\) is determined by membrane parameters. In this linear model, \(I_{e}\) shifts the steady state but does not change \(\tau _{m}\).
derivation.unitsCheck: \(C/G_{L}\) has units of seconds, \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) has units of volts, \(t/\tau _{m}\) is dimensionless, and every additive term in the solution is a voltage.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(G_{L}\to 0\), \(\tau _{m}\to \infty\) and the standard form must reduce to the ideal-capacitor equation. When \(I_{e}=0\), \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}\).

workedExample.title: Rise and recovery during a current pulse
workedExample.problem: Let \(C=200 \mathrm{pF}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(E_{L}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\). Starting at rest, inject 100 pA for 40 ms, then remove it. Find voltage at 40 ms and again 20 ms later.
steps: \(\tau _{m}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), and during the pulse \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65 \mathrm{mV}+100 \mathrm{pA}/10 \mathrm{nS}=-55 \mathrm{mV}\).
After removal, the new steady state is −65 mV and the deviation at removal is 8.65 mV.
After another \(20 \mathrm{ms}=1\tau _{m}\), the deviation is \(8.65e^{-1}\approx 3.18 \mathrm{mV}\), so \(V\approx -61.82 \mathrm{mV}\).
workedExample.result: Voltage is approximately −56.35 mV at pulse offset and −61.82 mV 20 ms after removal.
workedExample.sanityCheck: During the rise, voltage must remain between −65 and −55 mV. During recovery, it must lie between −56.35 and −65 mV.

selfCheck.prompt: If C and \(G_{L}\) both double, how do \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) and \(\tau _{m}\) change?
selfCheck.answer: \(\tau _{m}=C/G_{L}\) remains unchanged. For the same total current \(I_{e}\), \(I_{e}/G_{L}\) is halved, so \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) moves closer to \(E_{L}\). If input also doubles in proportion to area, the steady-state offset can remain unchanged.

pitfalls: Combining \(\tau _{m}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) into one parameter effect instead of distinguishing response speed from steady state.
Forcing V to reset to \(E_{L}\) when current ends, which violates continuity of capacitor voltage.

modules.title: Derive the exact F–I curve from threshold crossings
modules.guidingQuestion: How does constant current become firing rate through an exponential threshold-crossing time, and why do the near-threshold and strong-input regimes have different shapes?
paragraphs: After each spike, reset voltage to \(V_{R}\). With constant input and no additional state variables, each subthreshold trajectory repeats the previous cycle. Threshold can be crossed only if \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\). The critical current follows from \(E_{L}+I_{T}/G_{L}=V_{T}\): \(I_{T}=G_{L}(V_{T}-E_{L})\). At or below this value, voltage approaches a subthreshold steady state asymptotically and firing rate is zero.

Set \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{R}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\) equal to \(V_{T}\) to obtain period \(\Delta t=\tau _{m} \ln[(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})]\) and frequency \(f=1/\Delta t\). This relation is not linear. As \(I_{e}\) approaches \(I_{T}\), the denominator voltage difference approaches zero and \(\Delta t\) diverges. At larger \(I_{e}\), the period shortens and approaches the linear strong-input approximation of a perfect integrator.

Add an absolute refractory period \(\delta\): after each spike, no integration occurs during a fixed wait, so total period is \(\delta +\Delta t\) and \(f=1/(\delta +\Delta t)\). For very large input, \(\Delta t\to 0\) and firing rate approaches \(1/\delta\) instead of increasing without bound. This is a falsifiable limit. A model with no refractory period cannot consistently claim a finite maximum rate.

A common biased threshold-linear approximation is \(f\approx [wI+b]_{+}\). It can summarize an F–I curve over a limited operating range, but it does not preserve the logarithmic onset near rheobase and does not generate \(1/\delta\) saturation automatically. Report the fitted range and determine w and b from the exact curve or data; do not mistake the approximation for the exact LIF solution.
keyPoints: LIF fires periodically only when \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\), equivalently \(I_{e}>I_{T}\).
The exact period contains the natural logarithm of a ratio of voltage differences.
The refractory period limits the strong-input firing rate to \(1/\delta\).
A threshold-linear F–I curve is a local approximation and does not retain the full dynamics.

derivation.title: LIF period and strong-input limit
derivation.setup: Assume constant \(I_{e}>I_{T}\) and immediate reset to \(V_{R}\) after each threshold crossing. Derive the cycle first without a refractory period and then with \(\delta\).

steps.title: Write the post-reset trajectory
steps.explanation: \(V(t)=V_{\mathrm{inf}}+(V_{R}-V_{\mathrm{inf}})e^{-t/\tau _{m}}\), where \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=E_{L}+I_{e}/G_{L}\).

steps.title: Impose threshold
steps.explanation: Set \(V(\Delta t)=V_{T}\) to obtain \(e^{-\Delta t/\tau _{m}}=(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})\).

steps.title: Solve for the period
steps.explanation: Taking the logarithm gives \(\Delta t=\tau _{m} \ln[(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{R})/(V_{\mathrm{inf}}-V_{T})]\), and frequency is its reciprocal.

steps.title: Add the refractory period
steps.explanation: Add the fixed nonspiking interval to the charging time: \(f=1/(\delta +\Delta t)\).

steps.title: Check the strong-input limit
steps.explanation: For very large \(I_{e}\), \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\) is large. Using \(\ln(1+x)\approx x\) gives \(\Delta t\approx C(V_{T}-V_{R})/I_{e}\). If \(\delta >0\), \(f\to 1/\delta\).

symbolNotes: \(\Delta t\) is the charging time from reset to the next threshold crossing; \(\delta\) is the additional absolute refractory period.
\(I_{T}\) is the current that places the subthreshold steady state exactly at threshold, not the amplitude of an instantaneous current pulse.
derivation.unitsCheck: A ratio of voltage differences is dimensionless, as is its logarithm; multiplication by \(\tau _{m}\) gives time, and frequency has units \(s^{-1}=\mathrm{Hz}\).
derivation.limitCheck: As \(I_{e}\downarrow I_{T}\), \(f\to 0\). As \(I_{e}\to \infty\) with \(\delta =0\), f becomes approximately proportional to \(I_{e}\). With \(\delta >0\), \(f\to 1/\delta\).

workedExample.title: Calculate an F–I point with a refractory period
workedExample.problem: Let \(\tau _{m}=20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(E_{L}=V_{R}=-65 \mathrm{mV}\), \(V_{T}=-50 \mathrm{mV}\), \(G_{L}=10 \mathrm{nS}\), and \(\delta =2 \mathrm{ms}\). For \(I_{e}=200 \mathrm{pA}\), calculate \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}\), charging time, total period, and firing frequency.
steps: \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-65+200/10=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), and \(I_{T}=150 \mathrm{pA}\), so the neuron can fire.
The ratio of voltage differences is \((-45+65)/(-45+50)=20/5=4\).
The charging time is \(\Delta t=20 \ln 4\approx 27.73 \mathrm{ms}\).
Total period is \(27.73+2=29.73 \mathrm{ms}\), giving frequency \(1000/29.73\approx 33.64 \mathrm{Hz}\).
workedExample.result: \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}=-45 \mathrm{mV}\), charging time 27.73 ms, total period 29.73 ms, and frequency approximately 33.6 Hz.
workedExample.sanityCheck: With a refractory period, 33.6 Hz must be below the approximately 36.1 Hz value without one and far below the ceiling \(1/0.002=500 \mathrm{Hz}\).

selfCheck.prompt: Why can a complex or negative time returned by the crossing formula when \(I_{e}<I_{T}\) not be interpreted as an unusual form of spiking?
selfCheck.answer: The derivation assumes \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\), making the logarithmic ratio a positive number greater than 1. At a subthreshold steady state, the trajectory never crosses threshold; an expression outside its domain simply signals that the assumption failed.

pitfalls: Applying the logarithmic formula without first checking \(V_{\mathrm{inf}}>V_{T}\).
Confusing charging time with total period and omitting the absolute refractory interval.
Interpreting the intercept of a threshold-linear approximation as one specific biological membrane parameter.

modules.title: Hodgkin–Huxley gating, area normalization, and spatial propagation
modules.guidingQuestion: How do variable ionic conductances produce action potentials and refractory periods, and how does a point-neuron equation extend across membrane area and axonal space?
paragraphs: The Hodgkin–Huxley membrane equation is \(C dV/dt=I_{e}-G_{L}(V-E_{L})-\bar{G}_\mathrm{Na} m^{3}h(V-E_{\mathrm{Na}})-\bar{G}_K n^{4}(V-E_{K})\). \(\bar{G}\) is maximal conductance when every relevant gate is open; \(m^{3}h\) and \(n^{4}\) are open fractions. Each branch still has the form “conductance × driving force,” but voltage-dependent gating variables now modulate conductance dynamically.

A two-state gate n obeys \(dn/dt=\alpha _{n}(V)(1-n)-\beta _{n}(V)n\). The first term is closed fraction times opening rate; the second is open fraction times closing rate. Rearranging gives \(dn/dt=-(\alpha +\beta )n+\alpha\). Define \(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\) and \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\) to obtain \(\tau _{n} dn/dt=-n+n_{\mathrm{inf}}\). At fixed voltage, n approaches that voltage's steady-state open fraction exponentially.

During the action-potential upstroke, rapid growth of Na activation m produces inward Na current and positive feedback. Na inactivation h falls with depolarization while K activation n rises more slowly; together they terminate the upstroke and repolarize the membrane. After a spike, h has not recovered and n remains elevated, making another depolarization difficult. This is the kinetic origin of refractoriness. It differs from the fixed \(\delta\) imposed in LIF, although \(\delta\) can approximate its rate-limiting effect.

To compare cell sizes, substitute \(C=c_{m}A\), \(\bar{G}_x=\bar{g}_xA\), and \(I=iA\) and divide by A to obtain an area-normalized membrane equation. Doubling area while keeping current density and channel density fixed leaves voltage dynamics unchanged. Keeping total injected current fixed gives a larger cell lower current density and a smaller voltage response. State whether an experiment controls total current or current density.

A single-compartment model assumes uniform voltage throughout the cell. A multicompartment model writes one membrane equation per segment and couples neighbors by axial currents. Passive subthreshold perturbations decay with distance because axial current continually leaks across the membrane. An action potential, however, activates voltage-gated Na channels in the next segment and regenerates. Different combinations of channel type, density, morphology, and time constant produce diverse firing patterns, while charge conservation and gating logic remain reusable.
keyPoints: HH current still equals conductance times driving force; gating variables regulate the instantaneous conductance.
\(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\) sets speed, while \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\) sets the target at fixed voltage.
Na activation, Na inactivation, and delayed K activation together generate the action potential and refractory period.
Area normalization separates total parameters from densities; multicompartment coupling separates passive decay from active regeneration.

derivation.title: Derive standard gating-variable form from transition rates
derivation.setup: Consider many identical gates, each closed or open. Let n be the open fraction, \(\alpha\) the closed-to-open rate, and \(\beta\) the open-to-closed rate.

steps.title: Write inflow and outflow
steps.explanation: The closed fraction is 1−n, so open-state inflow per unit time is \(\alpha (1-n)\); open-state outflow is \(\beta n\).

steps.title: Collect terms in n
steps.explanation: Expansion gives \(dn/dt=\alpha -(\alpha +\beta )n\).

steps.title: Solve the steady state
steps.explanation: Set \(dn/dt=0\) to obtain \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\), which lies between 0 and 1.

steps.title: Identify the time constant
steps.explanation: Let \(\tau _{n}=1/(\alpha +\beta )\), giving \(\tau _{n} dn/dt=-n+n_{\mathrm{inf}}\).

steps.title: Write the fixed-voltage solution
steps.explanation: With fixed \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), \(n(t)=n_{\mathrm{inf}}+[n(0)-n_{\mathrm{inf}}]e^{-t/\tau _{n}}\).

symbolNotes: \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are transition rates with units of inverse time and depend on membrane voltage.
n is a fraction, not a channel count. Under independent gating, \(n^{4}\) is the probability that four n gates are open simultaneously.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(dn/dt\) has units 1/time, matching \(\alpha (1-n)\) and \(\beta n\). \(\tau _{n}\) has units of time, while n and \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\) are dimensionless.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\beta =0\), \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=1\) and the gate eventually opens fully. If \(\alpha =0\), \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=0\) and it eventually closes fully. Multiplying \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) by the same factor leaves steady state unchanged but speeds the response.

workedExample.title: Opening of a gating variable after a voltage-clamp step
workedExample.problem: At a fixed voltage, \(\alpha =0.3 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), \(\beta =0.1 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}\), and \(n(0)=0.2\). Find \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\), \(\tau _{n}\), n after 5 ms, and the change in \(n^{4}\).
steps: \(\tau _{n}=1/0.4 \mathrm{ms}^{-1}=2.5 \mathrm{ms}\).
Initially \(n^{4}=0.2^{4}=0.0016\); after 5 ms, \(0.6756^{4}\approx 0.2084\), an increase of about 130-fold.
workedExample.result: \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}=0.75\), \(\tau _{n}=2.5 \mathrm{ms}\), \(n(5 \mathrm{ms})\approx 0.676\), and \(n^{4}\) rises from 0.0016 to about 0.208.
workedExample.sanityCheck: \(n(5 \mathrm{ms})\) must lie between initial value 0.2 and steady state 0.75; every gating fraction lies between 0 and 1.

selfCheck.prompt: If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both double, why does \(n_{\mathrm{inf}}\) remain fixed while \(\tau _{n}\) is halved?
selfCheck.answer: Steady state depends only on the ratio \(\alpha /(\alpha +\beta )\), so the common factor cancels. The time constant is the reciprocal of total transition rate; doubling both rates halves the relaxation time.

pitfalls: Treating m, h, and n as currents or voltages instead of gate-open fractions between 0 and 1.
Judging current magnitude from reversal potential alone while ignoring an instantaneous gated conductance that may be nearly zero.
Mixing total current, total conductance, and per-area density when comparing cells of different membrane area.

objectives: Explain how the analysis moves from the mechanisms that generate action potentials to observable spike sequences, and identify which single-cell details are retained or averaged away in a coding analysis.
Interpret the stimulus, MT recording, spike train, raster, and PSTH in a random-dot motion experiment, and calculate firing rates by hand from raw counts.
Use the Fano factor and the coefficient of variation of interspike intervals to distinguish count variability from interval variability, and state the statistical object measured by each.
Derive the window-count and waiting-time distributions of a homogeneous Poisson process, and explain how a constantly driven LIF neuron differs from Poisson spiking.
Write the likelihood, log-likelihood, maximum-likelihood estimate, and Fisher information for a population of independent Poisson neurons, and relate likelihood curvature to estimation uncertainty.
prerequisiteBridge: Earlier lectures treated membrane voltage as a continuous state that produces a discrete spike when it crosses threshold. Coding analyses often stop tracking the millivolt waveform of each action potential and instead record the time \(t_{k}\) of every spike or the spike count n in a fixed window. This compression is appropriate when asking whether a response distinguishes stimuli, but a count alone is insufficient when the question concerns spike shape, dendritic location, or channel pharmacology. First establish what the observation discards; only then can you tell how far the conclusion generalizes.

A frequency in Hz is the number of events per second. If n spikes are observed in a window lasting T seconds, the single-window rate estimate is n/T. Across repeated trials, the rate in a PSTH bin is the total number of spikes in that bin divided by trial count×bin width. Narrower bins provide finer temporal resolution, but contain fewer events and therefore fluctuate more. Convert milliseconds to seconds before plotting or calculating, or the result will be wrong by a factor of 1000.

The mean describes the center of a distribution, whereas the variance describes its spread across repeated trials. The Fano \(\mathrm{factor}=\mathrm{variance}/\operatorname{mean}\) applies to counts obtained with a fixed stimulus and fixed time window; CV=standard deviation/mean is commonly applied to adjacent interspike intervals within one spike sequence. Poisson counts have equal mean and variance, so \(\mathrm{Fano}=1\). Exponential waiting times have equal mean and standard deviation, so \(CV=1\). A value near 1 is a reference point, not proof that a real neuron is exactly Poisson.

A likelihood holds the observed response fixed and treats the stimulus or parameter as the candidate being compared. Independence turns a joint probability into a product of neuron-wise probabilities; taking the logarithm turns that product into a sum, simplifying computation and separating each neuron's contribution of evidence. A zero first derivative locates the likelihood peak, while the second derivative describes its sharpness. The sharper the peak, the faster nearby candidates lose support and, in general, the more precise the estimate.

diagnostic.prompt: A 20 ms PSTH bin contains a total of 8 spikes across 10 trials. What is the firing rate in that bin?
diagnostic.answer: The total observation time is \(10\times 0.020=0.20 \mathrm{s}\), so the rate is \(8/0.20=40 \mathrm{Hz}\).
diagnostic.explanation: The PSTH denominator includes both the number of trials and the bin width. Dividing only by 20 ms would yield a rate based on the count pooled across trials, not the mean rate per trial.

diagnostic.prompt: At a fixed stimulus, the count mean is 4 and the variance is 6. What is the Fano factor, and how should it be interpreted relative to a Poisson process?
diagnostic.answer: \(\mathrm{Fano}=6/4=1.5\), which is above the Poisson reference value of 1 and is called overdispersion. This number alone does not identify the underlying mechanism.
diagnostic.explanation: Slow state changes, uncontrolled stimulus variables, correlated inputs, and nonstationary rates can all increase count variance. Distinguishing them requires additional experiments or model comparisons.

diagnostic.prompt: A homogeneous Poisson process has rate \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\). What is the probability of observing zero spikes in \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\)?
diagnostic.explanation: Window counts follow \(a \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda )\) distribution, where \(\lambda\) must equal rate times time. Exponential waiting times and Poisson window counts are two views of the same process.

diagnostic.prompt: A deterministic LIF neuron receives constant current and is reset to the same \(V_{R}\) after every spike. Why does it not naturally generate exponentially distributed ISIs?
diagnostic.answer: Every cycle has the same initial value, input, and dynamics, so threshold is crossed after a fixed time and the ISI is nearly constant. Random ISIs require stochastic input, a fluctuating threshold, or another source of noise.
diagnostic.explanation: The Poisson assumption is a statistical model of event generation; it does not follow automatically from the use of an integrate-and-fire neuron.

modules.title: From channel dynamics to coding observables
modules.guidingQuestion: When the question changes from “How are spikes generated?” to “What do spikes represent?”, which mechanisms still constrain the code, and which details can temporarily be compressed?
paragraphs: Na activation, Na inactivation, K activation, and the refractory period constrain observable spike sequences: the absolute refractory period imposes a lower bound on adjacent interspike intervals, recovery of gating variables introduces history dependence, and conductances and morphology shape the stimulus-to-spike transformation. Thus, even a coding model that uses only counts cannot permit unbounded firing rates or negative counts. Compressed mechanisms remain present as boundary conditions on the statistical description.

Parameters per unit area, axonal propagation, and cell diversity also affect the data. Applying the same total current to cells with different areas produces different current densities, while different channel combinations produce tonic, bursting, or adapting response patterns. If multiple cell types are pooled into one “average neuron” category, count variance may reflect differences among cell types rather than intrinsic randomness within a cell. Experimental grouping is therefore a necessary step before specifying a probabilistic model.

A coding problem must define the stimulus variable s and response variable n. The stimulus s might be motion direction, coherence, or sound frequency; n might be a single-window count, a complete spike train, or a vector of counts across neurons. Different choices retain different information. Keeping only the total count over 200 ms prevents testing whether the stimulus mainly alters precise within-window timing; retaining every event time increases both model complexity and data requirements.

Moving from a mechanistic model to a statistical model does not declare channel details “unimportant”; it marginalizes them for a specified task and timescale. Once spikes can be detected reliably, for example, event times can replace action-potential shape, and a conditional firing rate can summarize fast intracellular variables. If the statistical law fails systematically, return to the mechanistic level to investigate refractory effects, adaptation, common input, or nonstationary stimuli. Productive analysis moves back and forth between these levels.
keyPoints: Refractoriness and the history of gating variables impose physiological bounds on spike statistics.
The response can be represented by counts, event times, or population vectors; that choice determines which questions can be answered.
A statistical model is a task-directed compression of mechanistic variables, not a denial that those mechanisms exist.

workedExample.title: Checking a proposed firing rate against the refractory period
workedExample.problem: A neuron has an absolute refractory period of at least 2 ms. A model predicts a mean of 80 spikes in a 100 ms window. Use an upper-bound calculation to decide whether the prediction is possible.
steps: An absolute refractory period of 2 ms means adjacent spikes must be separated by at least 0.002 s.
The idealized maximum sustained rate is \(1/0.002=500 \mathrm{Hz}\).
In 100 ms, the neuron can emit at most about \(0.1\times 500=50\) spikes. Conventions about the endpoints of the window can change this by only about one event.
A predicted mean of 80 already exceeds the physical maximum, so the model is missing an essential constraint even before it is fit to data.
workedExample.result: 80 spikes/100 ms equals 800 Hz, exceeding the approximately 500 Hz upper bound imposed by a 2 ms refractory period.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Shortening the window should reduce the maximum event count in direct proportion to its duration. Because 100 ms is one tenth of 1 s, its upper bound is about one tenth of the per-second bound.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does an accurate count model not establish that precise spike timing contains no additional information?
selfCheck.answer: It establishes only that counts suffice for the chosen task. To determine whether timing adds predictive information beyond counts, compare the count model with a model that retains timing on independent data.

pitfalls: Compressing each action-potential waveform to an event and then claiming that the model explains channel dynamics.
Mistaking variance caused by pooling cell types or stimulus states for intrinsic randomness under a fixed condition.

modules.title: Random-dot motion, rasters, PSTHs, and trial-to-trial variability
modules.guidingQuestion: How can repeated extracellular voltage recordings be converted into a time-dependent mean response without erasing variability across trials?
paragraphs: A random-dot motion stimulus controls motion direction and coherence: some dots move together while the rest move randomly. When recording an MT neuron, an extracellular electrode measures fast voltage waveforms that are converted into spike times by a consistent detection rule. Motion direction, coherence, recording window, and behavioral task are all conditioning variables. If they change across trials, the spikes cannot simply be pooled into one “average response.”

Each row of a raster represents one trial, each tick represents one spike, and the horizontal axis is time relative to stimulus onset. A raster displays both mean temporal structure and trial differences. If many rows become denser around 100 ms after stimulus onset, the conditional rate has increased during that period; variation in event counts and times across rows shows that repeated responses are not deterministic trajectories. A raster is not a rate curve: visual density must be converted to a normalized count before experiments can be compared.

A PSTH partitions time into bins, totals the spikes in each bin across all trials, and divides by the number of trials K and bin width \(\Delta t\): \(\hat{r}_{b}=N_{b}/(K\Delta t)\). It estimates the trial-averaged rate under that condition. Narrow bins localize fast changes but have small, noisy \(N_{b}\) values; wide bins are smoother but mix distinct temporal phases. Choose and report a bin width that matches the timescale of the hypothesis being tested.

Trial-to-trial variability can be quantified in a fixed window using the count \(\operatorname{mean} \mu _{N}\) and variance \(\sigma _{N}^{2}\), with Fano \(\mathrm{factor}=\sigma _{N}^{2}/\mu _{N}\). The Poisson reference is 1; values greater than 1 are relatively overdispersed, and values less than 1 are relatively regular. The Fano factor changes with window length, stimulus alignment, and latent state, so it should never be reported without its condition. Plot the count distribution as well, because identical means and variances can arise from very different tails or mixture structures.
keyPoints: A raster retains individual-trial events; a PSTH estimates the time-varying rate averaged across trials.
The PSTH denominator is trial count times bin duration in seconds, giving a result in Hz.
The Fano factor compares count variance with count mean, but its interpretation depends on a fixed condition and window.

derivation.title: Constructing a PSTH rate estimate from total bin counts
derivation.setup: The same stimulus is repeated K times. Time bin b has width \(\Delta t\), and the count in that bin on trial k is \(N_{kb}\).

steps.title: Pool exposure under the same condition
steps.explanation: The total count is \(N_{b}=\sum _k N_{kb}\), and the total observation time is \(K\Delta t\).

steps.title: Divide by total time
steps.explanation: A rate is the number of events divided by exposure time, so \(\hat{r}_{b}=N_{b}/(K\Delta t)\).

steps.title: Relate the estimate to the single-trial mean
steps.explanation: The mean count per trial in this bin is \(N_{b}/K\). Dividing by \(\Delta t\) gives the same expression.

steps.title: Quantify uncertainty
steps.explanation: If trials are independent and Poisson within this bin, \(\operatorname{Var}(N_{b})=K r_{b}\Delta t\), so the standard deviation of the rate estimate is approximately \(\operatorname{sqrt}[r_{b}/(K\Delta t)]\).

symbolNotes: \(N_{kb}\) is a dimensionless nonnegative integer, K is the number of trials, and \(\Delta t\) must be entered in seconds.
\(r_{b}\) is the conditional firing rate, assumed approximately constant within the bin; the hat denotes an estimate from data.
derivation.unitsCheck: Counts are dimensionless, so division by \(K\Delta t\) gives \(s^{-1}=\mathrm{Hz}\). The standard-deviation expression also reduces to Hz.
derivation.limitCheck: As K grows, fluctuations in the estimate shrink as \(1/\sqrt K\). Making \(\Delta t\) too small leaves most bins empty and increases variance, although temporal resolution improves.

workedExample.title: Calculating both a PSTH rate and a count Fano factor
workedExample.problem: Across 10 trials, one 20 ms bin contains a total of 8 spikes. In a separate analysis of the full 200 ms window, the ten trial counts are \([1,2,3,2,2,1,4,2,1,2]\). Calculate the bin rate, the mean full-window count, the variance defined with 1/K, and the Fano factor.
steps: The bin's total exposure time is \(10\times 0.020=0.20 \mathrm{s}\), so its PSTH rate is \(8/0.20=40 \mathrm{Hz}\).
The full-window counts sum to 20, so \(\mu =20/10=2\).
The squared deviations from the mean are \([1,0,1,0,0,1,4,0,1,0]\), whose sum is 8. Using 1/K gives variance \(8/10=0.8\).
\(\mathrm{Fano}=0.8/2=0.4\), below the Poisson reference. An unbiased sample variance would instead use denominator K−1, so the convention must be reported.
workedExample.result: PSTH-bin rate: 40 Hz; window-count mean: 2; variance: 0.8; Fano factor: 0.4.
workedExample.sanityCheck: An average of 2 spikes over the full 200 ms window corresponds to 10 Hz. This does not conflict with a 40 Hz instantaneous bin because the PSTH can vary over time.

selfCheck.prompt: Why can concatenating all trials into one long spike train before making a histogram conceal important structure?
selfCheck.answer: Concatenation discards alignment to each stimulus onset and the identity of each trial. It can no longer separate time-locked changes in the mean, trial-to-trial count variability, and slow state drift, and it may create artificial intervals at concatenation boundaries.

pitfalls: Dividing a PSTH only by bin width and omitting trial count, thereby inflating the rate by a factor of K.
Entering 20 ms as 20 s, producing a factor-of-1000 unit error.
Examining only the smooth PSTH average and ignoring the trial distribution visible in the raster.

modules.title: Poisson coding, maximum likelihood, and Fisher curvature
modules.guidingQuestion: When neural responses are stochastic, how can a decoder be built from stimulus-conditional distributions, and how does likelihood curvature quantify the precision with which the stimulus can be localized?
paragraphs: A homogeneous Poisson point process assumes that the probability of one event in any very short interval dt is approximately r dt, disjoint intervals are independent, and the probability of two or more events is of higher order. It follows that the count N in a window of length T is Poisson with \(\operatorname{mean} \lambda =rT\). The probability that a waiting time exceeds t is the probability of no preceding event, \(e^{-rt}\), so the ISI density is r \(e^{-rt}\). Its mean and standard deviation are both 1/r, giving \(CV=1\).

An encoding model should specify the conditional distribution \(P(n|s)\), not merely a mean relation \(n=f(s)\). For MT neuron i, a tuning curve \(f_{i}(\theta )\) can specify the mean rate at direction \(\theta\), with \(N_{i}|\theta \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(f_{i}(\theta )T)\) in a window T. Two directions may produce the same mean in one neuron and therefore be ambiguous; a population with different preferred directions can break this degeneracy through its joint response.

If neurons are conditionally independent given \(\theta\), the population likelihood is a product of neuron-wise terms. Its log-likelihood is ℓ(θ)=Σ_i[N_i ln(f_i(θ)T)−f_i(θ)T−ln(N_i!)]. The maximum-likelihood estimate \(\theta _{\mathrm{hat}}\) is the direction under which the observed counts are most probable. Factorial terms that do not depend on \(\theta\) may be omitted when finding the maximum, but they still matter when calculating normalized probabilities or comparing different datasets.

Near the true \(\theta _{0}\), the log-likelihood can be approximated by a downward-opening quadratic. Fisher information is the negative expected second derivative, \(J(\theta )=-E[\ell ''(\theta )]\). A large J means a sharp peak and good discrimination among nearby directions. Under regularity conditions and with large samples, the maximum-likelihood estimate is approximately normal with variance about 1/J. This is an asymptotic scaling relation; with finite data, use repeated simulation or bootstrap analysis to examine bias and tails.

Poisson spiking is a useful baseline, not a default truth. Real neurons have refractory periods, adaptation, nonstationary rates, and correlations across neurons, all of which violate independent homogeneous assumptions. A useful diagnostic sequence proceeds from single-unit count distributions and ISI survival curves to Fano/CV measures and population noise correlations. The form of model failure should guide revision, instead of using a more complicated distribution to conceal inadequate experimental control.
keyPoints: A homogeneous Poisson process produces both Poisson window counts and exponential ISIs.
An encoding model specifies \(P(n|s)\); decoding holds the response fixed and compares likelihoods across s.
For an independent population, the log-likelihood is the sum of the evidence contributed by individual neurons.
Fisher information is expected negative curvature, and asymptotic estimation variance is approximately its reciprocal.

derivation.title: Fisher information for a population of independent Poisson neurons
derivation.setup: Neuron i has an independent Poisson count \(N_{i}\) in a window T, with \(\operatorname{mean} \lambda _{i}(\theta )=f_{i}(\theta )T\). Derive the Fisher information about stimulus \(\theta\).

steps.title: Write the log-likelihood
steps.explanation: Independence turns the logarithm of the joint probability into a sum.

steps.title: Take the first derivative
steps.explanation: Differentiating with respect to \(\theta\) while holding T constant gives \(f_{i}'(\theta )[N_{i}/f_{i}(\theta )-T]\) for each term.

steps.title: Take the second derivative and its expectation
steps.explanation: The second derivative contains \(f_{i}''\) multiplied by \([N_{i}/f_{i}-T]\), whose expectation is zero because \(E[N_{i}]=f_{i}T\). The remaining term supplies the negative curvature.

steps.title: Obtain the information
steps.explanation: Taking \(-E[\ell '']\) gives \(J(\theta )=T\sum _i[f_{i}'(\theta )]^{2}/f_{i}(\theta )\).

steps.title: Interpret the scaling
steps.explanation: Contributions from independent neurons add, and information grows linearly with observation time T. The asymptotic standard deviation shrinks as \(1/\sqrt J\).

symbolNotes: \(f_{i}(\theta )\) has units of Hz, \(f_{i}'(\theta )\) has units of Hz per stimulus unit, and T is measured in seconds.
J has units of inverse squared stimulus units, so \(1/\sqrt J\) has the same units as \(\theta\).
derivation.unitsCheck: \(T\cdot (\mathrm{Hz}/\theta )^{2}/\mathrm{Hz}=(s\cdot s^{-1})/\theta ^{2}=1/\theta ^{2}\), the required units of information.
derivation.limitCheck: If every \(f_{i}'(\theta )=0\), mean responses are locally unchanged by the stimulus and \(J=0\). Replicating independent neurons with identical tuning makes J proportional to their number.

workedExample.title: Estimating a constant Poisson rate from repeated counts
workedExample.problem: The same condition is presented 5 times. Each trial lasts \(T=0.2 \mathrm{s}\), and the counts are \([1,3,2,0,4]\). Assuming a shared constant Poisson rate r, find its maximum-likelihood estimate and the probability of zero spikes in one 0.2 s window.
steps: The total count is \(1+3+2+0+4=10\), and the total exposure is \(5\times 0.2=1.0 \mathrm{s}\).
The part of the log-likelihood that depends on r is \(10 \ln r-r\cdot 1.0\), whose first derivative is 10/r−1.0.
Setting the derivative to zero gives \(\hat{r}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\). Because the second derivative is \(-10/r^{2}<0\), this is a maximum.
For one 0.2 s window, the mean is \(\lambda =\hat{r} T=2\), so \(P(N=0)=e^{-2}\approx 0.1353\).
workedExample.result: The maximum-likelihood rate is 10 Hz; the model assigns a probability of about 13.5% to zero spikes in one window.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Because the total observation time is exactly 1 second and the total count is 10, the intuitive count rate is 10 Hz. With \(\lambda =2\), the zero-count probability should be less than \(e^{-1}\).

selfCheck.prompt: Why does taking the logarithm of a product of likelihood terms leave the location of the maximum-likelihood estimate unchanged?
selfCheck.answer: The natural logarithm is strictly increasing on positive numbers, so it preserves the ordering of candidate likelihoods. Taking logs only changes products into sums and improves numerical stability; it does not change the maximizer.

pitfalls: Interchanging \(P(n|s)\) and \(P(s|n)\) without specifying a prior or normalization.
Declaring that all assumptions of an independent homogeneous Poisson process hold merely because \(\mathrm{Fano}\approx 1\) and \(CV\approx 1\).
Applying the Fisher-information formula directly near \(f_{i}(\theta )=0\) without checking regularity and differentiability.

objectives: Explain how a population with diverse preferred directions resolves ambiguities in single-neuron tuning, and write the population Poisson likelihood.
Derive Fisher information from the population log-likelihood, distinguishing the contributions of neuron count N, observation time T, and tuning-curve shape.
State the assumptions of the Cramér–Rao lower bound and relate perceptual error to neural decoding precision without treating the bound as achieved performance.

Calculate the variance of pooled correlated counts, use the inverse covariance matrix to explain harmful noise along the signal direction, and distinguish the existence of correlation from a limitation on information.
Derive the bias–variance decomposition and explain how biased or Bayesian decoders can trade prior-induced bias for reduced variance.
prerequisiteBridge: The previous lecture derived the information in an independent Poisson population, \(J(\theta )=T\sum _i[f_{i}'(\theta )]^{2}/f_{i}(\theta )\). Each term asks how quickly a neuron's mean response changes under a small stimulus change relative to its own Poisson variability. A neuron can fire vigorously at the peak of its tuning curve yet be locally insensitive because the derivative is zero. Responses on the slope often contribute more local information because they change faster. Information is not a synonym for mean firing rate.

Variance measures the spread of an estimate across repeated datasets. An unbiased estimator has a mean estimate equal to the true stimulus. Under regularity conditions, the Cramér–Rao lower bound states that the variance of any unbiased estimator cannot be less than 1/J. This is a theoretical floor: it neither guarantees that a practical decoder reaches the floor nor captures every finite-sample bias. When comparing a behavioral threshold with \(1/\sqrt J\), specify stimulus units, trial count, observation time, and decoding assumptions.

A covariance matrix C places each neuron's noise variance on the diagonal and shared fluctuations off the diagonal. The long axis of a two-dimensional ellipse is a direction of greater noise. The mean-response displacement caused by changing the stimulus, \(\mu '(s)\), is also a direction in population space. Noise is harmful when the long axis aligns with \(\mu '\), not simply when a pairwise correlation coefficient is positive or negative. Multiplication by \(C^{-1}\) downweights directions with large noise.

A biased estimator need not average to the truth over repeated datasets. Its mean-squared error, MSE, is the sum of variance and squared bias. Pulling an estimate moderately toward common stimuli may therefore exchange a small bias for a larger reduction in variance. Bayesian decoding produces this pull through a prior \(P(s)\). A prior is not an arbitrary embellishment: it should express how often stimuli occur in the task environment and is multiplied by the current trial's likelihood to form the posterior.

diagnostic.prompt: One neuron has the same mean rate for directions \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Why might a population still distinguish the two directions?
diagnostic.answer: Other neurons with different preferred directions can have different mean response patterns under \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The resulting joint response vectors have different probabilities, so the population pattern resolves the single-neuron degeneracy.
diagnostic.explanation: Decoding uses the conditional distribution of the entire response vector; it does not classify each neuron separately and then take a vote.

diagnostic.prompt: If the number of independent neurons with identical tuning shapes increases from N to 4N while everything else remains fixed, how do Fisher information and asymptotic standard deviation scale?
diagnostic.answer: Information increases by a factor of 4, while standard deviation shrinks as \(1/\sqrt J\) to 1/2 of its original value.
diagnostic.explanation: Independent evidence adds, so \(J\propto N\). Error is measured on the standard-deviation scale, the square root of variance, and therefore improves only as \(\sqrt N\).

diagnostic.prompt: Why is the statement “The neurons are positively correlated, so coding information must decrease” incorrect?
diagnostic.answer: Whether a correlation is harmful depends on the alignment of covariance with the direction in which the stimulus changes the mean response. Positive-correlated noise that lies mainly orthogonal to the signal direction can have little effect.
diagnostic.explanation: Use \(\mu '^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}\mu '\) or an equivalent geometric analysis; the sign of one Pearson correlation coefficient is not enough.

diagnostic.prompt: An estimator has bias \(b=-0.3\) and variance 0.5. What is its MSE?
diagnostic.answer: \(MSE=\operatorname{Var}+b^{2}=0.5+0.09=0.59\).
diagnostic.explanation: Bias is squared before it is added to variance. Positive and negative biases contribute equally to MSE, although the direction remains scientifically meaningful.

modules.title: Population decoding and the N and T scaling of Fisher information
modules.guidingQuestion: How do neurons with translated tuning curves jointly localize a stimulus, and why do adding neurons and lengthening the observation time increase information in the same way?
paragraphs: A single bell-shaped tuning curve can give the same firing rate on either side of its peak, so count \(k_{i}\) may have equal likelihood under directions \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Neuron i in a population has preferred direction \(\theta _{i}\) and tuning \(f_{i}(\theta )=f(\theta -\theta _{i})\). Although the two stimuli are degenerate for one neuron, they produce different count patterns across other neurons. The joint probability compares the entire pattern, allowing distributed preferences to resolve a single neuron's ambiguity.

In a window T, the independent Poisson likelihood is Π_i[(f_i(θ)T)^{k_i}e^{−f_i(θ)T}/k_i!]. Taking the logarithm converts the product to a sum, whose derivative is the score. At the true \(\theta\), the negative expected second derivative contains terms with \(f_{i}''\) that vanish because \(E[k_{i}]=f_{i}T\), leaving \(J(\theta )=T\sum _i[f_{i}'(\theta )]^{2}/f_{i}(\theta )\). Each neuron's local evidence is nonnegative and the contributions add.

Suppose N preferred directions \(\theta _{i}=2\pi _{i}/N\) are uniformly spaced on the circle and N is large. The sum can be approximated by a Riemann integral: \(\sum _i F(\theta _{i})\approx N\int _{0}^{2\pi }F(\vartheta )d\vartheta /(2\pi )\). Because every tuning curve is a translation of the same shape, a change of variables makes the integral independent of the current \(\theta\). Thus J equals N T times a constant determined only by tuning shape, and a uniform population has approximately equal local precision at all directions.

For large samples, the maximum-likelihood estimate is approximately \(N(\theta _{0},1/J)\). Information therefore grows linearly with N and T, variance falls as 1/(NT), and standard deviation falls as \(1/\sqrt{NT}\). Observation time must be multiplied by four to halve the standard deviation. This scaling relies on independence and stable tuning; common noise, drift, and neural redundancy can alter additivity.

If a model predicts that information grows without bound with N but behavioral or neural performance saturates, at least three explanations are possible: correlation structure is information-limiting, the recorded neurons do not represent the population actually read out, or the biological decoder is suboptimal. Saturation alone cannot select among these explanations; discriminating covariance and decoding experiments are needed.
keyPoints: A population resolves single-neuron tuning ambiguity through the joint pattern of neurons with different preferred directions.
Independent Poisson information is \(T\sum _i(f_{i}')^{2}/f_{i}\).
For a large uniform population, replacing a sum with an integral gives \(J\propto NT\) and error standard deviation∝\(1/\sqrt{NT}\).

derivation.title: From a sum over uniformly spaced preferred directions to a continuous integral
derivation.setup: Consider N independent Poisson neurons with \(\theta _{i}=2\pi _{i}/N\), \(f_{i}(\theta )=f(\theta -\theta _{i})\), and \(J(\theta )=T\sum _i[f_{i}'(\theta )]^{2}/f_{i}(\theta )\).

steps.title: Define the summed function
steps.explanation: Let \(F(u)=[f'(u)]^{2}/f(u)\), so \(J(\theta )=T\sum _i F(\theta -\theta _{i})\).

steps.title: Insert the grid spacing
steps.explanation: The uniform spacing is \(\Delta \theta =2\pi /N\). Rewrite the sum as \(N/(2\pi )\) times a Riemann sum.

steps.title: Use periodic translation
steps.explanation: Tuning is periodic on the direction circle. With \(u=\theta -\vartheta\), changing \(\theta\) only translates the integration interval, and the integral over one complete period is unchanged.

steps.title: Separate scaling from shape
steps.explanation: This gives \(J(\theta )\approx NT j_{f}\), where \(j_{f}=(1/2\pi )\int _{0}^{2\pi }[f'(u)]^{2}/f(u)du\).

steps.title: Convert information to an error scale
steps.explanation: The asymptotic variance is approximately \(1/(NTj_{f})\), and the standard deviation is approximately \(1/\sqrt{NTj_{f}}\).

symbolNotes: \(\theta\), \(\theta _{i}\), and u are all direction variables; when angles are measured in radians, one period is \(2\pi\).
\(j_{f}\) contains only the shape, baseline, and amplitude of one tuning curve; it does not contain N or T.
derivation.unitsCheck: If \(\theta\) is measured in radians, \(j_{f}\) has units \(\mathrm{Hz}/\mathrm{rad}^{2}\). Multiplication by T seconds and N gives \(1/\mathrm{rad}^{2}\), whose inverse square root has units rad.
derivation.limitCheck: If tuning is constant, \(f'=0\) and \(j_{f}=0\). When N is small, the integral approximation can depend on direction and the discrete sum must be retained.

workedExample.title: A numerical comparison of information scaling
workedExample.problem: Suppose the mean shape constant contributed by one uniformly tuned neuron is \(j_{f}=0.8 \mathrm{rad}^{-2}s^{-1}\). For \(N=100\) and \(T=0.5 \mathrm{s}\), calculate J and the asymptotic standard deviation; then increase N to 400.
steps: Under the original condition, \(J=NTj_{f}=100\times 0.5\times 0.8=40 \mathrm{rad}^{-2}\).
The standard deviation is approximately \(1/\sqrt 40\approx 0.1581 \mathrm{rad}\), or about 9.06°.
The new standard deviation is \(1/\sqrt 160\approx 0.0791 \mathrm{rad}\approx 4.53\)°, exactly half the original value.
workedExample.result: Increasing N from 100 to 400 raises J from 40 to 160 and lowers error standard deviation from about 9.1° to 4.5°.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Quadrupling neuron count halves standard deviation, consistent with square-root scaling. The units change from \(\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\) for information to rad for error.

selfCheck.prompt: Why need a high firing rate at the peak of a tuning curve not contribute the greatest local Fisher information?
selfCheck.answer: The Poisson information term is \((f')^{2}/f\). Although f is large at the peak, the slope f' is generally zero, so the mean barely changes under an infinitesimal stimulus change and local information may be zero.

pitfalls: Equating information with total spike count and ignoring tuning slope.
Replacing a sum with an integral for a very small or nonuniform population without checking the approximation error.
Inferring directly from \(J\propto N\) in an independent model that biological performance must improve without limit.

modules.title: The CRLB, noise correlations, and information limits
modules.guidingQuestion: When do correlated fluctuations disappear through population averaging, and when do they persist along the signal direction and constrain every decoder?
paragraphs: For a differentiable model with regular support and an unbiased estimator, the Cramér–Rao lower bound gives \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{s})\ge 1/J(s)\). It constrains any decoding method, not only maximum likelihood, but it does not guarantee attainability at finite sample size and does not directly apply to biased estimators. Comparing \(1/\sqrt J\) with a psychophysical discrimination threshold can test whether the recorded population contains enough information; it cannot prove that the animal uses an optimal readout.

First distinguish two kinds of “correlation.” Signal correlation compares conditional means or tuning shapes across stimuli. Noise correlation fixes the stimulus and compares trial-wise deviations from each neuron's conditional mean. Only the latter enters the present pooling variance. Suppose the \(N_{R}\) residuals in a right-choice pool each have variance \(\sigma _{R}^{2}\) and every distinct pair has correlation \(c_{R}\). The variance of the pool average R is \(c_{R}\sigma _{R}^{2}+(1-c_{R})\sigma _{R}^{2}/N_{R}\). The independent component disappears as \(N_{R}\) grows, but the shared residual remains.

This saturation of pooling demonstrates that correlations can limit a particular readout; it does not establish that optimal population information must also saturate. With a uniform correlation structure, simple averaging may discard discriminable differences along with noise, whereas an optimal linear or nonlinear decoder may exploit other directions. Distinguish information-limiting correlations, models that saturate only for extremely large N, and performance saturation caused by a suboptimal decoder.

More generally, suppose a count vector k at stimulus s is approximately Gaussian, \(N(\mu (s),C)\), and C is temporarily assumed independent of s. The stimulus-dependent part of the log-likelihood is \(-(k-\mu )^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}(k-\mu )/2\), and Fisher information is \(J=\mu '^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}\mu '\). This is Mahalanobis geometry: changes in the mean along high-noise eigen-directions are downweighted, while changes along low-noise directions are amplified.

Information-limiting noise specifically means shared fluctuations that are indistinguishable from a change in the signal. For example, a noise component along \(\mu '(s)\) makes the population response appear as if the stimulus itself shifted slightly. Adding more similar neurons cannot readily average away that component. Neither positive nor negative correlation is a sufficient criterion. Compare the eigenvectors of the covariance with \(\mu '\), and keep biological information, the recorded subpopulation, and the actual decoder conceptually distinct.
keyPoints: The CRLB is a variance lower bound under explicit regularity and unbiasedness assumptions, not an automatic equality with observed error.
The variance of an equicorrelated pool average retains the \(c\sigma ^{2}\) term, so simple pooling can saturate as N grows.
Under a Gaussian approximation, \(J=\mu '^{\mathrm{T}}C^{-1}\mu '\); the effect of correlation depends jointly on noise direction and signal direction.

derivation.title: Variance of the average of equicorrelated residuals after fixing the stimulus
derivation.setup: At fixed stimulus s, let \(\epsilon _{i}=k_{i}-E[k_{i}|s]\) be the trial residual of neuron i. Assume \(\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon _{i}|s)=\sigma ^{2}\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon _{i},\epsilon _{j}|s)=c\sigma ^{2}\) for any \(i\ne j\), and define the residual pool average \(R=N^{-1}\sum _i\epsilon _{i}\).

steps.title: First remove conditional means
steps.explanation: Subtracting the mean at each stimulus condition removes signal correlation caused by common changes in tuning curves and leaves only noise residuals under a fixed condition.

steps.title: State the noise covariance assumption
steps.explanation: Diagonal entries are residual variances; off-diagonal entries are shared residuals at a fixed stimulus.

steps.title: Expand the variance of the pool average
steps.explanation: The constant \(N^{-1}\) is squared and taken outside; the double sum then covers every i,j pair.

steps.title: Separate diagonal and off-diagonal terms
steps.explanation: There are N variance terms and \(N(N-1)\) ordered covariance terms. Positive correlation does not automatically cancel in the sum.

steps.title: Simplify and take the limit
steps.explanation: Substitution and simplification show that, for fixed \(c>0\), the shared residual creates a floor that does not vanish with N.

symbolNotes: Signal correlation describes similarity of conditional means across stimuli; noise correlation describes shared trial residuals after s is fixed.
c is the residual correlation coefficient. An equicorrelation covariance matrix must remain positive semidefinite.
R is a simple arithmetic average, not an optimal decoder, so the derivation describes only the variance of this projection.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\epsilon\), k, and R are counts; c is dimensionless, while \(\sigma ^{2}\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(R|s)\) have units of counts squared.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(c=0\), variance falls as 1/N; when \(N=1\), it reduces to \(\sigma ^{2}\); and with fixed \(c>0\), a floor remains as N becomes large. If different stimuli are pooled before correlation is calculated, the result includes both signal and noise and cannot be substituted into this expression.

workedExample.title: Quantifying the pooling floor caused by shared fluctuations
workedExample.problem: There are \(N=100\) similar neurons, each with count variance \(\sigma ^{2}=4\), and every pair has correlation \(c=0.1\). Calculate the variance of their pool average and compare it with the independent case.
steps: The shared term is \(c\sigma ^{2}=0.1\times 4=0.4\).
The averageable term is \((1-c)\sigma ^{2}/N=0.9\times 4/100=0.036\).
The total variance is \(0.4+0.036=0.436\).
If \(c=0\), the variance is only \(4/100=0.04\). The correlated model is about 10.9 times larger.
workedExample.result: The correlated pool-average variance is 0.436, compared with 0.04 for the independent pool; most error comes from the 0.4 term that does not disappear with N.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The result should be less than the single-neuron variance 4 but greater than the independent average 0.04; 0.436 satisfies both checks.
